26 September 2026 — No plane through the vertex line carries its order, but two planes do at p = 3

Refutation of both planar relaxations for every p ≥ 3 (explicit products); at p = 3 the vertices of the two planes together lift the jet (finite check); conjecture for all p. Cycle bmd-r68. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The endpoint lemma puts every boundary witness \(P_p\) in \(J^{\,p}\), \(J=(x_1-x_2,x_3)\) the ideal of the line \(L\) through \(0\) and \(v=(1,1,0)\), while conj:cube-boundary-witness-vertex-order asks for \(J^{\psi(p)}\), \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\). The endpoint lemma entry proposed a sufficient relaxation on the plane \(x_1=x_2\): keep only the multiplicities at that plane's nonzero vertices and the jet at the origin. Is it true? If not, which vertices must a proof use? The test ends with a counterexample for every \(p\), or a proof target.

Setting. Boundary parameters: \(\ell=p^2-1\), \(m=4p\), \(k=\ell+m+1=p^2+4p\), \(D=2k-p\). Put \(K=k-p=p(p+3)\), which is even. For a set \(S\) of nonzero vertices, the \(S\)-relaxation at order \(j\) is the statement: every \(P\) of degree \(\le D\) with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the points of \(S\) and \(P\equiv A\pmod{\mathfrak m_0^k}\) for some \(A\in J^{\,j}\) lies in \(J^{\,j}\). By the jet statement of the endpoint lemma entry (the vertex-line lemma, part 1, with the boundary coordinate theorem and the order theorem), the \(S\)-relaxation at order \(\psi(p)\) for the seven nonzero vertices implies the conjecture for \(p\).

The endpoint bound is sharp on each plane

Proposition (ex:cube-plane-relaxation-sharpness). Over every field and for every \(p\ge1\), write \(u=x_1-x_2\) and \(a=K/2\). The polynomials

\[P_\Delta=u^p\,x_1^{a}(x_1-1)^{a}(x_3-x_1)^{a}(x_3+x_1-1)^{a},\qquad P_\square=x_3^p\,x_1^{a}(x_1-1)^{a}x_2^{a}(x_2-1)^{a}\]

have degree \(D\), lie in \(\mathfrak m_0^k\), lie in \(J^{\,p}\) but not in \(J^{\,p+1}\), and have multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the nonzero vertices of the plane \(x_1=x_2\) (for \(P_\Delta\)), respectively \(x_3=0\) (for \(P_\square\)), and multiplicity \(\ge K=k-p\) at every other vertex. Hence for \(p\ge3\), where \(\psi(p)\ge p+1\), the relaxation to either plane fails at order \(\psi(p)\), and more generally at every order \(j\ge p+1\). The endpoint lemma's order \(p\) is the exact answer for both plane relaxations.

Proof. Multiplicity at a point is additive over products, since the lowest homogeneous part of a product is the product of the lowest parts. A linear form contributes 1 at each point where it vanishes. For \(P_\Delta\): at \(0\) the factors \(u\), \(x_1\), \(x_3-x_1\) vanish, giving \(p+2a=k\). At \((1,1,0)\) they are \(u,x_1-1,x_3+x_1-1\), giving \(k\). At \((0,0,1)\) they are \(u,x_1,x_3+x_1-1\), giving \(k\). At \((1,1,1)\) they are \(u,x_1-1,x_3-x_1\), giving \(k\). At the off-plane vertices \(u=\pm1\), and exactly two of the four other factors vanish (for instance \(x_1-1\) and \(x_3+x_1-1\) at \((1,0,0)\)), giving \(2a=K\). For \(P_\square\): at \(0\) the factors \(x_3,x_1,x_2\) give \(k\). At \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\) and \((1,1,0)\) the factor \(x_3\) and two of the four others vanish, giving \(k\). At the vertices with \(x_3=1\) only two of the four vanish, giving \(K\). The degree is \(p+4a=p+2K=D\). The origin multiplicity \(k\) puts both in \(\mathfrak m_0^k\), so their jets there are \(0\in J^{\,j}\) for every \(j\). In coordinates \((x_1,u,x_3)\), \(J=(u,x_3)\). In \(P_\Delta=u^pG\) the factor \(G\) restricts on \(L=\{u=x_3=0\}\) to \(\pm x_1^{2a}(x_1-1)^{2a}\ne0\), so \(G\notin J\). Since \(J\) is generated by a regular sequence, \(J^{\,i}\) equals its symbolic power, so \(u^pG\notin J^{\,p+1}\). The same holds for \(P_\square=x_3^pG'\), with \(G'|_L=x_1^{2a}(x_1-1)^{2a}\). \(\square\)

So the input the conjecture needs beyond order \(p\) lives entirely in the vertices off the chosen plane. Both examples fail there by exactly \(p\) orders of multiplicity.

Which vertex sets lift the jet

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_vertex_line_witness.cpp gains two modes. relax takes the plane \(x_1=x_2\), and relaxmask takes any vertex set \(S\), given as a bitmask over \(v=v_1+2v_2+4v_3\). Unknowns are all coefficients of degree \(\le D\). The kernel compares the nullity under the \(S\)-multiplicities plus the jet rows (coefficients of \(x_1^au^bx_3^c\) with \(b+c<j\) and \(a+b+c<k\)) with the nullity when all such rows are imposed. Equal nullities mean the \(S\)-relaxation holds. Ranks are FLINT ranks over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\).

Finite check (check:cube-vertex-mask-relaxations, research/results/bmd-r68-plane-relaxations/). At \(p=3\), \(j=\psi(3)=4\), 11480 unknowns:

  • plane \(x_1=x_2\) (vertices \((1,1,0),(0,0,1),(1,1,1)\)): nullity 6020 with the jet rows, 6019 with all rows, so the relaxation fails by one dimension;
  • plane \(x_3=0\) (vertices \((1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,0)\)): 6020 against 6019, fails by one dimension;
  • both planes (five vertices, all but \((1,0,1)\) and \((0,1,1)\)): 2535 against 2535, holds;
  • all seven vertices: 53 against 53, holds.

At \(p=2\) (2300 unknowns, \(j=2\)) the plane \(x_1=x_2\) gives 1184 against 1184, as the endpoint lemma requires (positive control). The two failures have exactly the dimension of the proposition's examples. The memberships are certified only over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\): a holding relaxation there is evidence for characteristic 0, not a proof.

The two-plane lift

Conjecture (conj:cube-two-plane-lift). For every \(p\ge1\), in characteristic 0 and large characteristic, every \(P\) of degree \(\le D=2k-p\) with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the five nonzero vertices of the planes \(x_3=0\) and \(x_1=x_2\), and with \(P\equiv A\pmod{\mathfrak m_0^k}\) for some \(A\in J^{\psi(p)}\), lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\). It holds for \(p\le2\) by the endpoint lemma and is checked for \(p=3\) over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\). With the jet statement it implies conj:cube-boundary-witness-vertex-order.

In coordinates \((t,u,s)=(x_1,x_1-x_2,x_3)\) write \(P=\sum_{b,c}u^bs^cR_{bc}(t)\). The endpoint lemma kills \(R_{bc}\) for \(b+c<p\) and, for \(p\le b+c=i<\psi(p)\), leaves \(R_{bc}=t^{k-i}(t-1)^{k-i}S_{bc}\) with \(\deg S_{bc}\le i-p\). The two examples are the extreme directions \(u^p\) and \(s^p\) at level \(i=p\). Each is killed by the plane cut out by the other's variable: \(P_\Delta\) (factor \(u^p\)) fails on \(\{s=0\}\), at \((1,0,0)\) and \((0,1,0)\), and \(P_\square\) (factor \(s^p\)) fails on \(\{u=0\}\), at \((0,0,1)\) and \((1,1,1)\). A proof has to show that the two planes' conditions on the finitely many coefficients of the \(S_{bc}\), \(p\le b+c<\psi\), leave only zero.

General statement. ex:cube-plane-relaxation-sharpness, for every \(p\) and every field; conj:cube-two-plane-lift, for every \(p\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the endpoint lemma and its planar relaxation paragraph, the jet statement (vertex-line lemma part 1), and the boundary parameters. Claim searches (planar relaxation, vertex line, plane; product of linear forms, square diagonal) found no earlier version. The multiplicity count of both products was checked vertex by vertex, and it agrees with the computed one-dimensional defect of the \(x_1=x_2\) relaxation at \(p=3\). The positive control \(p=2\), where the endpoint lemma proves the relaxation, holds. A fresh-context referee checked the proposition at all eight vertices, the kernel's masks, jet rows and row counts, and the conjecture's implication, and found no mathematical error. Its corrections are made: the range \(i<\psi(p)\) for the endpoint factorization, the planes on which each example fails, and the finite-field qualification in the assessment.

Assessment. The planar relaxation proposed by the previous entry is false for every \(p\ge3\), and the reason is explicit: products of linear forms have exactly order \(p\) along the vertex line and are good on one plane. At \(p=3\), over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) (finite check), the vertices of the two planes together suffice, and the two remaining vertices are not needed. The conjecture's proof target is now a finite linear problem in the coefficients above the endpoint level, with two sets of plane conditions. Neither the order half nor tangent-cone independence moved. Process: one kernel extended, three runs, with a positive control and two predicted failures.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: the two-plane lift splits into rows and columns, and Horace peeling explains both

Route review; the two-plane lift decomposes into square problems that lift exactly below p, which covers p ≤ 4; faces of the cube peel (x_i − 1)^p. Cycle bmd-r69. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. Open statement 1: on \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)\ge B(d,\rho)\) for \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), through the sharp pair. The current line attacks its order half. At \((2e,2)\) the squeeze lemma needs two solutions of multiplicity \(\mu\) with independent tangent cones. Products of boundary witnesses supply them if each boundary witness lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\), \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\) (conj:cube-boundary-witness-vertex-order, through the vertex-line lemma).

What the goal needs. With the proved results, open statement 1 gives \(\delta_F(3,k,\ell)\) for all \(k,\ell\). The vertex-line conjecture for every \(p\) together with tangent-cone independence gives the order half at \((2e,2)\) only. Odd \(d\) and most \(\rho\ge3\) need non-product solutions (squeeze entry). Open statements 2 and 3 are the dimension \(n\ge4\) part.

Where the line stands. Since the last review:

  • The squeeze lemma turned the order half in tight cases into a construction problem.
  • Orders at double points became orders along vertex lines, which add under products (vertex-line lemma).
  • The endpoint lemma proved the vertex-line conjecture for \(p\le2\).
  • No single plane through the vertex line suffices for \(p\ge3\), but two planes do at \(p=3\) (two-plane lift).
  • In dimension 4, point windows stop at 14, below the threshold 19.

The vertex-line conjecture advanced from \(p\le2\) to a precise conjecture, but tangent-cone independence has not been touched, and odd \(d\) has no construction.

Falsification attempt

In coordinates \((t,u,s)=(x_1,x_1-x_2,x_3)\) write \(P=\sum_{b,c}u^bs^cR_{bc}(t)\). The multiplicity at a point of the plane \(u=0\) splits by the \(u\)-degree. So the conditions at the nonzero vertices of \(x_1=x_2\) say that each row \(Q_b=\sum_cs^cR_{bc}\) has multiplicity \(\ge k-b\) at \((t,s)=(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\). This is a square problem in which \(L\) is a side. Likewise the conditions at the nonzero vertices of \(x_3=0\) say that each column \(P_c=\sum_bu^bR_{bc}\) has multiplicity \(\ge k-c\) at \((t,u)=(1,1),(0,-1),(1,0)\). This is a square problem in which \(L\) is a diagonal. The origin jet hypothesis and the degree bounds are conditions on single entries. So the two-plane problem is a fibre product of row problems and column problems. If a row \(b\) forces its entries \(c<\psi-b\) to vanish, or a column \(c\) forces its entries \(b<\psi-c\) to vanish, then every pair \((b,c)\) with \(b+c<\psi\) that meets such a row or column is zero. Row \(b\) has degree deficiency \(e=p-b\): its degree bound is \(2(k-b)-e\).

The test computes, for each row and each column with index \(<\psi\), which entries below \(\psi-\) index some solution leaves nonzero (research/tools/bmd_cube_plane_rows.cpp, FLINT nullspaces over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), \(p=3,4,5,6\), 189 s; research/results/bmd-r69-route-review/plane-rows-p3-6.txt). It could have shown partial lifts, rows with scattered forced entries, or rows and columns behaving differently. The outcome is uniform, for every \(p\le6\):

  • every row and every column with index \(<p\) forces all its entries below \(\psi-\) index;
  • every row and every column with index \(\ge p\) forces none.

So the rows and columns cover all pairs \(b+c<\psi\) exactly when no pair has \(b,c\ge p\), that is when \(2p\ge\psi\), that is \(p\le4\). At \(p=3\) this reproduces the previous entry's two one-dimensional failures (row 3 and column 3). Granted the row and column statements, it gives the two-plane lift at \(p=4\). For \(p\ge5\) the uncovered block \(\{(b,c):b,c\ge p,\ b+c<\psi\}\) is decided by the coupling of rows and columns. At \(p=5\) the block is \(\{(5,5),(5,6),(6,5)\}\).

Assessment of this line

The vertex-line part is in good shape. The square problems behind it have a clean all-or-nothing behaviour, which the Horace lead below explains and turns into proofs. The face lead gives a new three-dimensional mechanism for \(p\ge5\), where two planes may not suffice. The risk has moved to the parts this line does not reach. Tangent-cone independence of the product solutions is still an open condition, and no non-product solutions exist for odd \(d\). Even a complete proof of the vertex-line conjecture gives the order half only at \((2e,2)\).

Outside leads

  • Fat points on the quintic del Pezzo surface (Harbourne, Complete linear systems on rational surfaces, Trans. AMS 289, 1985; the \(\le8\)-point case of the Segre–Harbourne–Gimigliano–Hirschowitz conjecture). The four vertices of a square are in linear general position. Their blow-up is a del Pezzo surface of degree 5, whose only \((-1)\)-curves are the exceptional divisors and the six lines. After the lines with negative intersection are removed, a system is non-special. This targets the square problems of the rows and columns, and gives their dimensions in closed form. It would break for the directional condition at the origin, which is a curvilinear scheme and not a fat point. Test. Passed: for six systems (multiplicity \(K\) at three vertices, \(m_0\) at the origin, degrees 36 to 60) the prediction (research/tools/bmd_route_review_r69_delpezzo.py) equals the computed dimension in every case: 16, 0, 0, 19, 441 and 388 (plain-dimensions.txt).
  • The Horace method (A. Hirschowitz, La méthode d'Horace pour l'interpolation à plusieurs variables, Manuscripta Math. 50, 1985; Alexander–Hirschowitz). Restrict to a line (the trace). When the trace system is empty, the line divides, and one continues with the residual. For a row with deficiency \(e\) use the two sides \(s=1\) and \(s=0\). On \(s=1\) the trace has degree \(\le2K-e\) and multiplicity \(K\) at both top vertices, so \((s-1)\) divides. Peeling \(r\) top factors and \(c\) bottom factors leaves the top trace empty while \(r<e+c\) and the bottom trace empty while \(c<e+r\). The bottom uses the multiplicity at \((1,0)\) and the directional origin condition. Each peel on one side adds one unit of slack on the other, so for \(e\ge1\) the process runs until \(s^j\mid Q\) for the whole jet order \(j\). For \(e\le0\) it never starts. The columns use \(L\) and the anti-diagonal \(x_1+x_2=1\) in the same way. This targets the two-plane lift through the rows and columns. It would break for the uncovered block, where \(e\le0\) in both directions. Test. Passed: the argument predicts exactly the computed all-or-nothing pattern, lifting below index \(p\) and failing from \(p\) on. Its full proof is written in the next research entry.
  • The multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel lemma on a face (Dvir–Kopparty–Saraf–Sudan, SICOMP 2013, Lemma 2.7). A nonzero polynomial with multiplicity \(\ge m\) at the four vertices of a square has degree \(\ge2m\). Equivalently, the six lines through pairs of vertices divide it whenever the degree is \(<2m\), and induction then applies. Take a polynomial of degree \(\le D=2k-p\) with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at all seven nonzero vertices. Its restriction to the face \(x_3=1\) therefore vanishes, so \((x_3-1)\mid P\). The same holds after each peel while \(D-r<2(k-r)\), that is \(r<p\). So \((x_1-1)^p(x_2-1)^p(x_3-1)^p\) divides every boundary witness. This targets the vertex-line conjecture for \(p\ge5\), where the far faces bring in the two vertices \((1,0,1),(0,1,1)\) that the two-plane problem omits. It would break if peeling the far faces does not feed slack to the faces through the origin. Test. Passed as a proof of the divisibility (the degree count above). Whether the peel reaches the origin faces is the next entry's question.

Absurd bridges

  • Product codes (coding theory: P. Elias, Error-free coding, 1954). The codewords of \(C_1\otimes C_2\) are the arrays whose rows lie in \(C_1\) and whose columns lie in \(C_2\). For a tensor product, a coordinate \((b,c)\) is identically zero exactly when \(b\) is outside the support of \(C_1\) or \(c\) is outside that of \(C_2\). The translation takes the array \((R_{bc})\) with its row and column problems. The two-plane problem is an irregular product, since each row and each column has its own code. If it behaved like a tensor product, the uncovered block would be unforced, and the two-plane lift would fail at \(p=5\). The smallest test is the three-dimensional two-plane system at \(p=5\). Test. Not run: that system has 109,736 unknowns, beyond a dense rank in this budget. The face lead makes it less pressing, since the conjecture may need all seven vertices anyway.
  • Discrete tomography (H. J. Ryser, 1957; Gale–Ryser). An array constrained by its rows and columns is non-unique exactly through switching components, alternating rectangles of free entries. The translation: a nonzero two-plane solution supported inside the uncovered block would be such a switching configuration of row and column solutions. The smallest test is the block's shape at the first \(p\) where it is nonempty. Test. Passed: at \(p=5\) the block \(\{(5,5),(5,6),(6,5)\}\) contains no rectangle, since \((6,6)\) has \(b+c=\psi\). So a counterexample at \(p=5\) must also use entries with \(b+c\ge\psi\), which the hypotheses do not constrain.

Next step

The next research entry writes the Horace peeling in full. It proves the row and column lemmas over every field, the two-plane lift for \(p\le4\), and hence the vertex-line conjecture for \(p\le4\) under the order theorem's hypotheses. It also proves the face divisibility, and tests whether peeling all six faces, with the directional condition at the origin, reaches \(J^{\psi}\) for every \(p\). Tangent-cone independence at \((4,2)\) comes after that.

Process. One small kernel (189 s), one dimension comparison and two proofs by degree count. The falsification test could have shown a scattered pattern and showed an all-or-nothing one.

26 September 2026 — Two-line peeling: the boundary witnesses vanish along the vertex line to order ⌊p²/2⌋ for p ≤ 6

Working proofs of the two-line peeling lemma and face divisibility; they prove the vertex-line conjecture for p ≤ 6 and the two-plane lift for p ≤ 4. Cycle bmd-r70. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review found that the two-plane problem splits into square problems for rows and columns, which lift exactly below index \(p\) (computed for \(p\le6\)). It proposed Horace peeling as the mechanism. Can the peeling be proved in general, and how far does it take conj:cube-boundary-witness-vertex-order (every boundary witness lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\), \(J=(x_1-x_2,x_3)\), \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\))? The test ends with a proof and the range of \(p\) it covers, or with the step where peeling stops.

The two-line peeling lemma

Lemma (lem:cube-two-line-peeling). Let \(F\) be any field. Let \(A=\{\alpha=0\}\) and \(B=\{\beta=0\}\) be distinct lines in \(F^2\) (\(\alpha,\beta\) affine linear). Take points \(a_1\ne a_2\) on \(A\setminus B\) and \(b_1\ne b_2\) on \(B\setminus A\), and integers \(d\), \(j\ge0\), \(M_1,M_2,N_1,N_2\). Let \(Q\in F[x,y]\) have degree \(\le d\), multiplicity \(\ge M_2\) at \(a_2\) and \(\ge N_i\) at \(b_i\), and suppose \(Q\in(\alpha^j)+\mathfrak m_{a_1}^{M_1}\). If \(M_1+M_2+N_1+N_2>2d\), then \(\alpha^j\mid Q\).

A multiplicity bound \(\le0\) is no condition. The ideal \((\alpha^j)+\mathfrak m_{a_1}^{M_1}\) is the directional condition: in affine coordinates \((\alpha,\tau)\) with \(\tau(a_1)=0\), writing \(Q=\sum_c\alpha^cR_c(\tau)\), it says \(\tau^{M_1-c}\mid R_c\) for \(c<j\). For \(j\ge M_1\) it is ordinary multiplicity \(\ge M_1\) at \(a_1\), and then \(\alpha^j\mid Q\) with \(j>d\) forces \(Q=0\).

Proof. A nonzero univariate polynomial of degree \(\le e\) vanishing to orders \(o_1,o_2\ge0\) at two distinct points has \(o_1+o_2\le e\). So the restriction of a bivariate polynomial of degree \(\le e\) to a line through two points is zero whenever its orders there sum to more than \(e\), and then the line's form divides the polynomial. Suppose \(Q=\alpha^c\beta^rQ'\) with \(0\le c\le j\), \(r\ge0\).

  • \(\alpha\) is a unit at \(b_i\) and \(\beta\) is a unit at \(a_i\). Multiplicity is additive over products. So \(Q'\) has multiplicity \(\ge N_i-r\) at \(b_i\) and \(\ge M_2-c\) at \(a_2\), and degree \(\le d-c-r\).
  • At \(a_1\), the ideal \((\alpha^j)+\mathfrak m_{a_1}^{M_1}\) is \(\mathfrak m_{a_1}\)-primary. So membership is decided in the local ring, where \(\beta^r\) is a unit. It is a monomial ideal in \((\alpha,\tau)\), so \(\alpha^cQ'\) lies in it exactly when \(Q'\in(\alpha^{j-c})+\mathfrak m_{a_1}^{M_1-c}\).

Put \(\sigma_A=M_1+M_2-d\) and \(\sigma_B=N_1+N_2-d\).

  • Top step. If \(r<\sigma_B+c\), the orders of \(Q'|_B\) at \(b_1,b_2\) sum to at least \(N_1+N_2-2r>d-c-r\). So \(\beta\mid Q'\), and \(r\) increases by one.
  • Bottom step. If \(c<j\) and \(c<\sigma_A+r\), the restriction \(Q'|_A\) is \(R'_0(\tau)\), which vanishes to order \(\ge M_1-c\) at \(a_1\) (since \(j-c\ge1\)) and \(\ge M_2-c\) at \(a_2\). These sum to more than \(d-c-r\), so \(\alpha\mid Q'\), and \(c\) increases by one.

Start with \(c=r=0\), \(Q'=Q\). While \(c<j\), some step applies: otherwise \(r\ge\sigma_B+c\) and \(c\ge\sigma_A+r\), whose sum gives \(\sigma_A+\sigma_B\le0\), against the hypothesis. Each step lowers the degree bound of \(Q'\) by one. If that bound becomes negative, then \(Q'=0\), so \(Q=0\). Otherwise the process reaches \(c=j\), and \(\alpha^j\mid Q\). \(\square\)

With ordinary multiplicity \(\ell\) at \(a_1\) and \(k\) at the other three vertices of the unit square, the lemma gives \(Q=0\) for \(3k+\ell>2d\). So the least degree is \(\ge2k-\lfloor(k-\ell)/2\rfloor\). This is the value of the square theorem, \(2k-\lceil(k-\ell-1)/2\rceil\), so the lemma is sharp there. It is also sharp for the directional condition: the sharpness examples have \(\sigma_A+\sigma_B=0\) in their rows and columns of index \(p\), and they are not divisible.

Face divisibility

Proposition (prop:cube-face-divisibility). Over any field, let \(P\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(n\ge2\), have degree \(\le D\) and multiplicity \(\ge k\) at every nonzero point of \(\{0,1\}^n\). Then \(\prod_i(x_i-1)^{\max(0,2k-D)}\) divides \(P\). For a witness with savings \(h\), \(D=n+2k-2-h\), so the exponent is \(h+2-n\). For the boundary witnesses on \(\{0,1\}^3\) it is \(p\).

Proof. The face \(x_i=1\) is a copy of \(\{0,1\}^{n-1}\) consisting of nonzero points. By the multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel lemma (Dvir–Kopparty–Saraf–Sudan, Lemma 2.7, with \(S=\{0,1\}\)), a nonzero polynomial of degree \(e\) in \(n-1\) variables with multiplicity \(\ge m\) at all of \(\{0,1\}^{n-1}\) has \(2^{n-1}m\le e\,2^{n-2}\), that is \(e\ge2m\). For \(n=2\), where the face is a pair of points on a line, this is the univariate count. If \(P=(x_i-1)^rP'\), then \(P'\) has multiplicity \(\ge k-r\) on the face and degree \(\le D-r\). The restriction of \(P'\) to the face has degree \(<2(k-r)\) while \(r<2k-D\), so it is zero, and \((x_i-1)\mid P'\). So \((x_i-1)^{2k-D}\mid P\) for each \(i\). The factors are pairwise coprime, so their product divides. \(\square\)

The vertex-line order

Theorem (thm:cube-vertex-line-order-small). Let \(p\ge1\), \(k=p^2+4p\), \(D=2k-p\), \(\psi=\psi(p)\). Use coordinates \((t,u,s)=(x_1,x_1-x_2,x_3)\), so that \(J=(u,s)\).

  1. Over any field, let \(P\) have degree \(\le D\), multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices of \(\{0,1\}^3\), and \(P\in J^{\psi}+\mathfrak m_0^k\). Then \(P\in J^{\psi}+(u^ps^{2p})\). Hence \(P\in J^{\psi}\) when \(3p\ge\psi\), that is for \(p\le6\).
  2. Over any field and for \(p\le4\), let \(P\) have degree \(\le D\), \(P\in J^{\psi}+\mathfrak m_0^k\), and multiplicity \(\ge k\) only at the five nonzero vertices of the planes \(x_3=0\) and \(x_1=x_2\). Then \(P\in J^{\psi}\). So conj:cube-two-plane-lift holds for \(p\le4\), over every field.
  3. Over a field of characteristic 0, or of odd characteristic \(q\) with \(q\nmid p\) or \(q=p\), every boundary witness \(P_p\) with \(p\le6\) lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\). So conj:cube-boundary-witness-vertex-order holds for \(p\le6\).

Proof. The expansion \(P=\sum_{b,c}u^bs^cR_{bc}(t)\) is used throughout.

  • Rows and columns. At a point of the plane \(u=0\), the multiplicity of \(P\) is \(\ge m\) if and only if each row \(Q_b=\sum_cs^cR_{bc}(t)\) has multiplicity \(\ge m-b\) there as a polynomial in \((t,s)\). The reason is that the local homogeneous parts of \(P\) are \(\sum_bu^b[Q_b]_{n-b}\), with distinct powers of \(u\). In the same way, at a point of \(s=0\) the columns \(P_c=\sum_bu^bR_{bc}(t)\) have multiplicity \(\ge m-c\) in \((t,u)\).
  • Origin condition. \(P\in J^\psi+\mathfrak m_0^k\) says \(t^{k-b-c}\mid R_{bc}\) for \(b+c<\psi\), a monomial condition in \((t,u,s)\). So \(Q_b\in(s^{\psi-b})+\mathfrak m_0^{k-b}\) and \(P_c\in(u^{\psi-c})+\mathfrak m_0^{k-c}\).

Part 1. By face divisibility, \(P=\Phi P'\) with \(\Phi=(x_1-1)^p(x_2-1)^p(x_3-1)^p\). Then \(P'\) has degree \(\le D-3p=2k-4p\). Its multiplicities are \(\ge k-p\) at the three vertices of weight 1, \(\ge k-2p\) at those of weight 2, and \(\ge k-3p\) at \((1,1,1)\). \(\Phi\) is a unit at \(0\) and \(J^\psi+\mathfrak m_0^k\) is \(\mathfrak m_0\)-primary, so \(P'\in J^\psi+\mathfrak m_0^k\).

  • Row \(b\) of \(P'\). Take \(A=\{s=0\}\) with \(a_1=0\) (directional, \(M_1=k-b\), \(j=\psi-b\)) and \(a_2=(1,1,0)\) (\(M_2=k-2p-b\)). Take \(B=\{s=1\}\) with \((0,0,1)\) (\(k-p-b\)) and \((1,1,1)\) (\(k-3p-b\)), and \(d=2k-4p-b\). The sum is \(4k-6p-4b>2d\) if and only if \(b<p\).
  • Column \(c\) of \(P'\). Take \(A=L=\{u=0\}\) with \(a_1=0\) (directional, \(M_1=k-c\), \(j=\psi-c\)) and \(a_2=(1,1,0)\) (\(k-2p-c\)). Take \(B=\{x_1+x_2=1\}\) with \((1,0,0)\) and \((0,1,0)\) (\(k-p-c\) each), and \(d=2k-4p-c\). Here \(u=\pm1\) at the points of \(B\), and \(x_1+x_2-1=\mp1\) at \(0\) and \((1,1,0)\). The sum is \(4k-4p-4c>2d\) if and only if \(c<2p\).

By the lemma, \(R'_{bc}=0\) whenever \(b+c<\psi\) and (\(b<p\) or \(c<2p\)). The remaining entries with \(b+c<\psi\) lie in \((u^ps^{2p})\), so \(P'\in J^\psi+(u^ps^{2p})\), and so is \(P=\Phi P'\). If \(3p\ge\psi\), every \(b+c<\psi\) has \(b<p\) or \(c<2p\), so \(P'\in J^\psi\) and \(P\in J^\psi\). The cases are \(\psi(p)=0,2,4,8,12,18\) for \(p\le6\), against \(\psi(7)=24>21\).

Part 2. Apply the lemma to \(P\) itself, with \(M_1=M_2=N_1=N_2=k-i\) and \(d=D-i=2(k-i)-(p-i)\) in row or column \(i\). The rows use \(A=\{s=0\}\) and \(B=\{s=1\}\); the columns use \(L\) and \(\{x_1+x_2=1\}\). The sum exceeds \(2d\) if and only if \(i<p\). So \(R_{bc}=0\) for \(b+c<\psi\) with \(\min(b,c)<p\), and \(2p\ge\psi\) holds for \(p\le4\). Only the five vertices were used.

Part 3. By the jet statement, \(P_p\in J^\psi+\mathfrak m_0^k\): this is the converse of part 1 of the vertex-line lemma, since every coordinate of the witness's solution vanishes to order \(\ge\psi(p)\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) by part 3 of the boundary coordinate theorem under the order theorem's hypothesis with \(d=p\). Part 1 applies. \(\square\)

The orders are exact: \(\operatorname{mult}F_p=\psi(p)\) for \(p\le7\) in characteristic 0 and 1000003 (check:cube-boundary-double-point-order-exact), and the top coordinate bounds the solution's multiplicity. For \(p\ge7\) the peeling leaves the block \(b\ge p\), \(c\ge2p\), \(b+c<\psi\), whose first entry is \((7,14)\) at \(p=7\). For boundary witnesses under the order theorem's hypothesis, the endpoint lemma's order \(\min(\psi,p)\) improves to \(\min(\psi,3p)\) for every \(p\), by part 1.

What it gives the order half. By the vertex-line entry, the products \(P_e^2\) and \(P_{e+1}P_{e-1}\) give the order half at \((2e,2)\) once their tangent cones are independent. They need the vertex-line order for \(p\in\{e-1,e,e+1\}\) and \(\operatorname{mult}F_p=\psi(p)\) there. Both now hold for \(e\le5\), that is \(d\in\{4,6,8,10\}\), in characteristic 0 (and in characteristic 1000003 for the exactness). Part 3 needs, for each \(p\in\{e-1,e,e+1\}\), odd characteristic \(q\) with \(q\nmid p\) or \(q=p\). This excludes, for instance, characteristic 3 at \(d=10\), where \(p=6\). Under these hypotheses, what remains open there is the tangent-cone independence alone.

General statement. lem:cube-two-line-peeling, for every field and all parameters; prop:cube-face-divisibility, for every \(n\); thm:cube-vertex-line-order-small, whose part 1 holds for every \(p\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the vertex-line lemma (part 1 and its converse), the boundary coordinate theorem (part 3), the order theorem's hypothesis, the multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel lemma, the square theorem's value, and the route review's row and column computation. Claim searches (Horace, peeling, trace, residual; square, four vertices, degree \(2m\)) found only Horace statements about PHP boards and the square theorem, which the lemma reproduces. Consistency checks: the lemma's criterion \(i<p\) for rows and columns of \(P\) is exactly the computed pattern for \(p\le6\) (research/results/bmd-r69-route-review/plane-rows-p3-6.txt), and parts 1 and 2 agree with the \(p=3\) mask computations of the plane relaxation entry. A fresh-context referee checked the lemma (invariants, the reduction at \(a_1\), termination, negative bounds), face divisibility, and the vertex bookkeeping, sums and case list of parts 1 and 2, including characteristic 2 for the column line. It found no mathematical error. Its corrections are made: the comparison with the endpoint lemma stated as \(\min(\psi,p)\) against \(\min(\psi,3p)\) under the order theorem's hypothesis; the characteristic hypotheses in the order-half paragraph and the field of the exactness check; and the full hypotheses of part 2.

Assessment. The vertex-line conjecture now holds for \(p\le6\), and for every \(p\) up to the block \(b\ge p\), \(c\ge2p\). A single degree count, the two-line peeling lemma, explains the square theorem's lower bound, the endpoint lemma, the plane relaxations and their failures. The order half at \((2e,2)\) for \(d\le10\) is reduced to the independence of two tangent cones. For \(p\ge7\) a further mechanism is needed, perhaps peeling through other planes or lines.

26 September 2026 — Product cones: the order half holds at (4,2), the first case with ρ ≥ 2

Working proof of the product cone formula; with an exact certificate over F_1000003 it proves the order half at (4,2) in characteristic 0 and 1000003. Cycle bmd-r71. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The vertex-line theorem leaves one open condition for the order half at \((2e,2)\), \(e\le5\). The squeeze lemma needs the solutions of the products \(P_e^2\) and \(P_{e+1}P_{e-1}\) to have independent tangent cones over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\) at the double point. How can those cones be computed, and are they independent at \(e=2\), that is at \((4,2)\)? The test ends with the cones in closed form and a decision at \((4,2)\).

The product cone formula

Setting. On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(J=(x_1-x_2,x_3)\) be the ideal of the line from \(0\) to \(v=(1,1,0)\), and use \((t,u,s)=(x_1,x_1-x_2,x_3)\). A polynomial \(P\in J^{\,j}\) has the normal form \(N_P=\sum_{a+b=j}u^as^bR_{ab}(t)\), its image in \(J^{\,j}/J^{\,j+1}\). Let \(L(x)=x^2-x\), \(r_0=L^{-1}\) (so \(r_0(0)=0\), \(r_0'(0)=-1\)), and \(\delta(\lambda)=L'(r_0(\lambda))^2L'(0)\), a unit of \(F[[\lambda]]\). Put

\[\tilde N_P(\lambda;U,S)=\sum_{a+b=j}R_{ab}(r_0(\lambda))\,r_0'(\lambda)^a(-1)^b\,U^aS^b.\]

At \(P_v=(1{:}1{:}0)\) use the chart \(y_2=1\), \(y_1=1+U\), \(y_3=S\). These are the local coordinates called \((t,s)\) in the squeeze lemma, renamed here to avoid a clash with \(t=x_1\), \(s=x_3\). Write \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\).

Lemma (lem:cube-product-cone-formula).

  1. Let \(P\) be a witness for \((k,\ell)\) with \(P\in J^{\,j}\), and \(m=k-\ell-1\). The degree-\(j\) part at \(P_v\) of the coordinate \(W_c\) of its solution is the coefficient of \(\lambda^{\ell+m-c-j}\) in \(\tilde N_P(\lambda;U,S)/\delta(\lambda)\). "Degree-\(j\) part" means the tangent cone when \(\operatorname{mult}_{P_v}W_c=j\), and zero when the multiplicity is larger.
  2. For a product \(P=\prod_iP_i\) with \(P_i\in J^{\,j_i}\), \(\tilde N_P=\prod_i\tilde N_{P_i}\).
  3. Let \(e\ge2\), and assume \(P_p\in J^{\psi(p)}\) for \(p\in\{e-1,e,e+1\}\). Put \(\mu_A=2\psi(e)\) and \(\mu_B=\psi(e+1)+\psi(e-1)\). For even \(e\) both equal \(e^2\); for odd \(e\) they are \(e^2-1\) and \(e^2+1\). Let \(w_A\), \(w_B\) be the solutions of \(P_e^2\) and \(P_{e+1}P_{e-1}\) at \(m=8e+1\). Their degree-\(\mu_A\) and degree-\(\mu_B\) parts are linearly dependent over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\) if and only if there is \(r\in F(\sigma,\tau)\) with \(\lambda^{-o_A}\tilde N_{P_e}^2\equiv r\,\lambda^{-o_B}\tilde N_{P_{e+1}}\tilde N_{P_{e-1}}\pmod{\lambda^{m+1}}\). Here \(o_A=\ell_A-\mu_A\) and \(o_B=\ell_B-\mu_B\), with \(\ell_A=2e^2-2\), \(\ell_B=2e^2\), are the orders of the top coordinates. In both parities \(\max(\mu_A,\mu_B)=\pi-\mu(2e,2)\) with \(\pi=\psi(2e)=2e^2\) and \(\mu(2e,2)=2\psi(e)\) (vertex-line entry). So, when these parts are independent and nonzero and \(\operatorname{mult}F_{2e}\ge\psi(2e)\), part 1 of the squeeze lemma gives the order half at \((2e,2)\).

Proof. Part 1. By part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma, \(W_c=[\tilde w]_{\ell+m-c}\) with \(\tilde w=v(r_0(y))/\prod_iL'(r_0(y_i))\), where \(v\) is the origin jet of \(P\). The components below degree \(k\) depend only on \(v\), so \(v\) may be replaced by \(P\). The vertex-line lemma shows that the substitution \(x=r_0(y)\) carries \(J\) to \(I_v=(y_1-y_2,y_3)\). Modulo \(I_v^{\,j+1}\) the three coordinates become:

  • \(u=r_0(y_1)-r_0(y_2)\equiv(y_1-y_2)\,r_0'(\lambda)\);
  • \(s=r_0(y_3)\equiv-y_3\);
  • \(t\equiv r_0(\lambda)\).

Here \(\lambda\) is the coordinate on the line \(y_1=y_2\), \(y_3=0\). The denominator restricts there to \(\delta(\lambda)\). So the image of \(\tilde w\) in \(I_v^{\,j}/I_v^{\,j+1}\) is \(\tilde N_P(\lambda;y_1-y_2,y_3)/\delta(\lambda)\). Its homogeneous part of degree \(n\) is the \(\lambda^{n-j}\) coefficient, with \(\lambda^{n-j}\) homogenized to \(y_1^{\,n-j}\). A form \(G\in I_v^{\,j}\) of degree \(n\) has, at \(P_v\), the degree-\(j\) part \(\sum t^as^bG_{ab}(1,1,0)\), where \(\sum(y_1-y_2)^ay_3^bG_{ab}\) is its image in \(I_v^{\,j}/I_v^{\,j+1}\). Taking \(n=\ell+m-c\) gives part 1. Part 2 holds because \(J^{\,j_1}J^{\,j_2}\subseteq J^{\,j_1+j_2}\), the normal forms multiply in the associated graded ring, and the substitution is a ring homomorphism.

Part 3. Both products are witnesses at \(m=8e+1\), with savings \(2e+1\) and origin orders \(\ell_A=2e^2-2\), \(\ell_B=2e^2\) (vertex-line entry). By parts 1 and 2 their degree-\(\mu_A\) and degree-\(\mu_B\) vectors, indexed by \(c=0,\ldots,m\), are the coefficients of orders \(\ell_A+m-c-\mu_A\) of \(\tilde N_A/\delta\) and \(\ell_B+m-c-\mu_B\) of \(\tilde N_B/\delta\). The top coordinate \(c=m\) sits at order \(o=\ell-\mu\) in each. So both vectors are the windows of orders \(0,\ldots,m\) of \(\lambda^{-o}\tilde N/\delta\). These are power series, because every term of \(R_{ab}\) has \(t\)-degree \(\ge\ell-\mu\) (origin order \(\ell\)). Two such windows are dependent over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\) exactly when one is \(r\) times the other, since each has a nonzero entry. Dividing by the common unit \(\delta\) changes neither dependence nor the congruence. For the last sentence, part 1 of the squeeze lemma gives \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge\pi-\max(\mu_A,\mu_B)\). For even \(e\) this is \(2e^2-e^2=e^2=2\psi(e)\), and for odd \(e\) it is \(2e^2-(e^2+1)=e^2-1=2\psi(e)\). \(\square\)

Reading at first order. The top cones are the tangent cones of \(F_e^2\) and \(F_{e+1}F_{e-1}\). By the lowest parts of the order theorem's branch product, the cone of \(F_p\) is a monomial in \(t,s\) for odd \(p\), and a monomial times \(t^p-s^p\) for even \(p\), where the multiplicity is exact. So for even \(e\) the top cone of \(w_A\) is a monomial times \((t^e-s^e)^2\), while that of \(w_B\) is a monomial, because \(e\pm1\) are odd. Then \(r\) is fixed and not constant. Dependence then forces \((U^e-S^e)^2\) to divide the coefficient of \(\lambda^{o_A+1}\) (one order above the top) of \(\tilde N_{P_e}^2/\delta\). That is a first-order test on \(P_e\) alone. In this paragraph \(t,s\) in the branch product are the chart coordinates \(U,S\). For odd \(e\) the binomials sit in the cone of \(w_B\), and the analogous test is on \(P_{e\pm1}\).

The order half at (4,2)

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_product_cones.cpp (FLINT) computes \(P_1,P_2,P_3\) modulo a prime as nullspace vectors: multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices, origin order \(\ge\ell\), degree \(\le2k-p\), with a nonzero degree-\(\ell\) part. It checks that their normal-form coefficients below \(\psi(p)\) cancel. It forms the series of the lemma, prints the cones of the top coordinates, and evaluates the \(2\times18\) matrix of degree-4 parts at five random points \((\sigma,\tau)\).

Finite check (check:cube-product-cones-four-two, research/results/bmd-r71-product-cones/). Over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\):

  • Each of \(P_1,P_2,P_3\) spans a one-dimensional space (nullity 1), and each lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\).
  • The top cones are \(-64(U^2-S^2)^2\) for \(P_2^2\) and \(1024\,U^2S^2\) for \(P_3P_1\), as the order theorem predicts.
  • The next cone of \(P_2^2\) (\(c=16\)) is \(-1664S^4+3584U^2S^2-1920U^4=(U^2-S^2)(1664S^2-1920U^2)\). It is not divisible by \((U^2-S^2)^2\).
  • The cones of \(P_3P_1\) at \(c=17,16\) are \(1024\,U^2S^2\) and \(28672\,U^2S^2\). So the minor on coordinates \(c=17,16\) is \(131072\,U^2S^2(U^4-S^4)=2^{17}U^2S^2(U^4-S^4)\) (computed from these coefficients as residues modulo \(q\)), which is nonzero. All five random evaluations have rank 2.
  • The control \(P_2^2\) against itself has rank 1 at all five points.

Theorem (thm:cube-order-half-four-two). Over a field of characteristic 0 or 1000003, every local solution at \((d,\rho)=(4,2)\) (\(m=17\)) vanishes to order \(\ge\mu(4,2)=4\) at each double point.

Proof. Over \(\mathbb Q\) the solution space of each \(P_p\) (\(p\le3\)) has dimension \(\ge1\) by the boundary theorem, and \(\le1\) because its rank cannot rise under reduction modulo \(q=1000003\). Take a primitive integral generator. Its reduction is a nonzero element of the one-dimensional space over \(\mathbb F_q\), so it is the computed \(P_p\) up to a scalar. Over \(\mathbb Q\) and over \(\mathbb F_q\), each \(P_p\) lies in \(J^{\psi(p)}\) by part 3 of the vertex-line theorem: \(p\le6\), in characteristic 0 or odd \(q\) with \(q\nmid p\), which holds for \(q=1000003\) and \(p\le3\). The kernel's modular check of the lower coefficients agrees with this. Every step of the lemma commutes with reduction:

  • normal forms;
  • \(r_0\), which has integer coefficients;
  • \(\delta^{-1}\), since \(\delta(0)=-1\).

So the \(2\times2\) minor on \(c=17,16\), a form over \(\mathbb Z_{(q)}\), reduces to a nonzero form, and it is nonzero over \(\mathbb Q\). The tangent cones of \(w_A,w_B\) are therefore independent over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\) for \(F\) of characteristic 0 or \(q\). This base change is faithfully flat, as in the squeeze lemma. Both have multiplicity exactly \(4=\mu\): their degree-4 parts are nonzero, and \(\operatorname{mult}\ge2\psi(2)=\psi(3)+\psi(1)=4\) by the vertex-line lemma. Part 1 of the squeeze lemma gives \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge\pi-4\) for every local solution \(W\), with \(\pi=\operatorname{mult}_PF_4\ge\lfloor16/2\rfloor=8\) by the order theorem (\(d=4\), odd characteristic never divides 4). So \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge4\) at \(P=(1{:}1{:}0)\). The double points are \((1{:}1{:}0)\), \((1{:}0{:}1)\) and \((0{:}1{:}1)\), one orbit of \(S_3\) permuting coordinates. The cube, the solution formula, and hence \(M\) and \(F_d\) are equivariant under these permutations. They map the unique boundary witnesses to themselves up to scalars, and so carry the whole argument to the other two double points. \(\square\)

The minor is a nonzero integral form, so the theorem also holds in all but finitely many odd characteristics. Which ones fail is not determined.

What it gives. The order half is the first half of the sharp pair at \((4,2)\), which is in the range of open statement 1 (\(d=4\), \(\rho=2\), \(B=6\), \(\mu=4\)). With the line-restriction bound, \(\ell_0(5,17)\ge6=B(4,2)\) now needs only the splitting half there: on a general line through a double point, the restricted solutions have minimal degree \(B-\mu=2\). The same method can prove the order half at \((2e,2)\) for \(3\le e\le5\) from the witnesses \(P_{e-1},P_e,P_{e+1}\), that is \(p\le6\). For even \(e=4\) the first-order test on \(P_4\) may suffice. Witnesses with \(p\ge4\) have 40,000 or more unknowns in the dense formulation, so they need the face-divided form \(\prod(x_i-1)^pP'\) with \(P'\in J^{\psi}+(u^ps^{2p})\).

General statement. lem:cube-product-cone-formula, for every witness in \(J^{\,j}\), every product and every \(e\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma, the vertex-line lemma, the squeeze lemma (part 1 and its setting), the order theorem's hypothesis and lowest parts, and the vertex-line entry's product parameters. Claim searches (tangent cone, product solution, independence) found only the squeeze lemma and the vertex-line entry, which pose the question. The kernel's control has rank 1. Its top cones agree with the order theorem's lowest parts, and its normal forms agree with the vertex-line theorem. A fresh-context referee checked part 1 (the transport of \(u,s,t\), \(\delta\), the degree-\(j\) parts), the kernel against the formula, the output residues and the minor (recomputed by hand), and the squeeze application. Its corrections are made: the vertex-line theorem cited for \(J^{\psi}\) membership over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb F_q\), the double points named with the equivariance, chart coordinates renamed \(U,S\), \(\psi\) defined, the first-order coefficient placed relative to the top order, and the forward claims restricted. It also read part 3 as false for odd \(e\), taking \(\mu(2e,2)=e^2\). The record's value is \(\mu(2e,2)=2\psi(e)=e^2-1\) for odd \(e\). Part 3 is now stated with the two degrees \(\mu_A\ne\mu_B\), and the squeeze bound \(\pi-\max(\mu_A,\mu_B)=2\psi(e)\) is checked in both parities.

Assessment. For the first time, the order half holds at a point with \(\rho\ge2\). The mechanism is general: normal forms along the vertex line multiply, and the cones are their Taylor windows. The decisive quantity is visible at first order. For \(3\le e\le5\) the obstacle is computational: witnesses for \(p=4,5,6\) in face-divided form. A general proof needs the first-order coefficient of the boundary solution's normal form, which the Tate model may give. The splitting half at \((4,2)\) is now the nearer target for a first case of open statement 1.

26 September 2026 — The first threshold inside open statement 1 (2 ≤ ρ ≤ d−1): ℓ₀(5,17) = B(4,2) = 6

Working proof that ℓ₀(5,17) = 6 in characteristic 0 and 1000003, from the sharp pair's two halves. Cycle bmd-r72. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The order half at \((4,2)\) is proved. Open statement 1 at \((4,2)\) asks for \(\ell_0(5,17)\ge B(4,2)=6\). By the line-restriction bound, this needs the splitting half on one line through a double point: no restricted solution of excess \(\beta-1=1\). Does the record already contain that, and in which characteristics does the conclusion hold? The test ends with the threshold proved or with the missing splitting datum.

The sharp pair gives the threshold

Lemma (lem:cube-sharp-pair-threshold). On \(\{0,1\}^3\), let \(1\le\rho\le d\), \(m=4d+\rho-1\), with \(\mu=\mu(d,\rho)\), \(\beta=\beta(d,\rho)=B(d,\rho)-\mu\) as in the sharp pair. Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Suppose:

  1. (order half) over \(\mathbb F_p\) and over a field of characteristic 0, every local solution at \(m\) vanishes to order \(\ge\mu\) at the double point \(P=(1{:}1{:}0)\), in every coordinate;
  2. (splitting datum) for one line \(L_0\) through \(P\) with integer coordinates, the restricted system over \(\mathbb F_p\) has \((E_{L_0})_{\beta-1}=0\).

Then \(\ell_0(d+1,m)=B(d,\rho)\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) and over every field of characteristic 0.

Proof. Global solutions are local solutions, so hypothesis 1 is the vanishing hypothesis of the line-restriction bound with \(k=\mu\). With hypothesis 2 and \(b=\beta\), that lemma gives \(\ell_0\ge\mu+\beta=B\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) and over every field of characteristic 0. The product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B\) in every characteristic \(\ne2\). The systems have coefficients in the prime field, so the dimension of each graded piece, and hence \(\ell_0\), is the same over every extension. The conclusion therefore holds over every field of characteristic \(p\), and over every field of characteristic 0. \(\square\)

This is the reduction that the sharp-pair entry stated in words, now as one lemma with a common setting. Hypothesis 2 is a single exact rank computation, and it is the only place where \(p\) enters apart from hypothesis 1.

The threshold at (4,2)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-four-two). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003, \(\ell_0(5,17)=B(4,2)=6\).

Proof. Here \(j=d-\rho=2\), \(q=2\), and the balanced partition of 4 into 2 parts is \((2,2)\). So \(\mu=2\lfloor4/2\rfloor=4\), \(\beta=2(\lceil4/2\rceil-1)=2\) and \(B=6\).

  • Hypothesis 1 is thm:cube-order-half-four-two, in characteristic 0 and 1000003.
  • Hypothesis 2 is in the saved output of check:cube-line-splitting (research/results/bmd-r45-mixed-lifts/line-splitting-generic-through-P.txt). For \(p=1000003\), \(d=4\), \(m=17\), \(\rho=2\) on the line through \(P=(1,1,0)\) and \(Q=(7,3,11)\), it lists \(\dim(E_L)_l=0\) for \(l\le1\) and \(\dim(E_L)_2=1\).

The lemma applies. \(\square\)

What it means for the degree. By the threshold-ideal lemma, \(\ell_0(h,m)\) is the initial degree of a homogeneous ideal \(I^{(h)}_m\), and the savings are \(h(k,\ell)=\max\{h:\ell_0(h,m)\le\ell\}\). A homogeneous ideal has nonzero forms in every degree at or above its initial degree and none below. So over fields of characteristic 0 or 1000003, along \(m=k-\ell-1=17\), the condition \(\ell_0(5,17)\le\ell\) holds exactly for \(\ell\ge6\). The savings are at least 5 for \(\ell\ge6\), that is \(\delta_F(3,\ell+18,\ell)\le2(\ell+18)-4\). For \(\ell\le5\) the savings \(h=5\) are not attained. Before this, the pre-stable thresholds with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) were known only as upper bounds, plus \(\ell_0\ge2\) from the order-zero theorem.

How far the recorded splitting data reach. check:cube-line-splitting gives \(b_{\min}=B-2(d-\rho)\) on the same line for \(3\le d\le7\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) except \((7,2)\). That is \(\beta\) exactly when \(\mu=2(d-\rho)\), that is when every part of the partition is at most 3. All parts are \(\le3\) if and only if \(j\le2q\), which is \(d\le3\rho\) when \(q=\rho\) and automatic when \(q=j\). In the computed range \(3\le d\le7\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), every case except \((7,2)\) has \(d\le3\rho\), and \((7,2)\) is the only case with \(d>3\rho\). So hypothesis 2 holds over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\) for every case of the computed range except \((7,2)\), and there the lemma reduces the threshold to the order half alone. The order half is proved at \((4,2)\). Through the squeeze lemma and the product cone formula, it is within reach at \((6,2)\) from face-divided witnesses \(P_2,P_3,P_4\). There \(d=6\le3\rho\), and the unequal cone degrees 8 and 10 still give \(\pi-10\ge18-10=8=\mu\). This is a prospect: the order half at \((6,2)\) is not proved.

General statement. lem:cube-sharp-pair-threshold, for every \((d,\rho)\) and every odd prime.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the line-restriction bound (its vanishing hypothesis for all global solutions, over \(\mathbb F_p\) and characteristic 0, and its excess convention), the sharp pair's \(\mu,\beta\), the product bound's range, the order half at \((4,2)\), and the saved splitting output. Its excess index \(l\) is the lemma's excess. Claim searches (torsion partition, threshold, order half, splitting) found only the conjectures and the prose reduction this lemma formalizes. A fresh-context referee recomputed \(\mu,\beta,B\) at \((4,2)\) and checked every block of the saved splitting output against the recorded check. It found the lemma, the theorem and the range claim correct. Its corrections are made: field extension for the conclusion, the fields and the initial-degree argument in the degree translation, \(\pi-10\ge8\) at \((6,2)\) as a prospect, the range stated exactly, the assessment limited to \((4,2)\), and the title restricted to \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) (the case \(\rho=d\) was proved earlier).

Assessment. Open statement 1 has its first proved case with \(2\le\rho\le d-1\). At \((4,2)\) the route is complete: product cones give the order half, the recorded splitting datum gives the rest, and the lemma turns the pair into the threshold. The splitting half is available as a finite datum in the computed range \(3\le d\le7\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\), \((d,\rho)\ne(7,2)\). There the remaining work is the order half, which product cones have proved only at \((4,2)\). It can go case by case through witnesses, or in general through the first-order coefficient of the normal forms. A proof for all \((d,\rho)\) still needs both halves in general.

26 September 2026 — Symmetric face-divided witnesses: the order half and the threshold at (6,2), ℓ₀(7,25) = 16

Working proof of the symmetry reduction for witnesses; with an exact certificate over F_1000003 it gives the order half at (6,2) and ℓ₀(7,25) = 16 in characteristic 0 and 1000003. Cycle bmd-r73. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The threshold at \((4,2)\) used witnesses \(P_1,P_2,P_3\). The next case in the range of the recorded splitting data that products can reach is \((6,2)\), where \(d=6\le3\rho\). The odd cases \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) are out of reach: at \((3,2)\) the only product is \(P_2P_1\), and at \((5,2)\) the products \(P_3P_2\) and \(P_4P_1\) have multiplicities 6 and 8, so the squeeze gives only \(\pi-8=4<\mu=6\). The case \((6,2)\) needs \(P_4\), which has about 40,000 unknowns in the dense formulation. Can the witnesses be computed in a reduced form, and are the product cones independent at \((6,2)\), where their degrees differ (8 and 10)? The test ends with the threshold at \((6,2)\) or with dependent cones.

The symmetry reduction

Lemma (lem:cube-witness-symmetry-reduction). Over a field \(F\) of characteristic not 2 or 3, for \(p\ge1\), \(k=p^2+4p\), \(D=2k-p\), \(\ell=p^2-1\), let \(V_p\) be the space of \(P\in F[x_1,x_2,x_3]\) with degree \(\le D\), multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices and origin order \(\ge\ell\).

  1. \(V_p=\Phi_p\cdot V'_p\), where \(\Phi_p=\prod_i(x_i-1)^p\) and \(V'_p\) is the space of \(P'\) with the following properties:
    • degree \(\le D-3p\);
    • origin order \(\ge\ell\);
    • multiplicity \(\ge k-pw(v)\) at each nonzero vertex \(v\) of weight \(w(v)\).
  2. The coordinate permutations act on \(V'_p\). Let \(n_{\rm triv}\), \(n_{\rm sgn}\) be the dimensions of its trivial and sign parts and \(n_{12}\) that of its \((12)\)-invariants. Then \(\dim V_p=n_{\rm triv}+n_{\rm sgn}+2(n_{12}-n_{\rm triv})\).
  3. If \(\dim V_p=1\), the witness spans \(V_p\) and is \(S_3\)-equivariant for the trivial or the sign character.

Proof. Part 1: by face divisibility, \(\Phi_p\mid P\) for \(P\in V_p\). The factor \((x_i-1)^p\) has multiplicity \(p\) at a vertex with \(x_i=1\) and is a unit at the others, and \(\Phi_p\) is a unit at the origin. Multiplicity is additive, so \(P'=P/\Phi_p\) has exactly the stated conditions, and conversely. Part 2: \(\Phi_p\) and the conditions are \(S_3\)-invariant, so \(S_3\) acts on \(V'_p\). In characteristic \(\nmid6\) the representation is semisimple, \(V'_p\cong\mathrm{triv}^{a}\oplus\mathrm{sgn}^{b}\oplus\mathrm{std}^{c}\), and a transposition fixes a one-dimensional subspace of the standard representation. So \(n_{12}=a+c\). Part 3 is immediate. \(\square\)

For \(P'\) in a character part, the multiplicity conditions need only one vertex per orbit: \((1,0,0)\), \((1,1,0)\) and \((1,1,1)\). For the \((12)\)-invariants, five representatives suffice. At \(p=4\) this reduces a dense system of about 40,000 unknowns to 3,642 (trivial part) and 10,353 (the \((12)\)-invariants).

The order half and the threshold at (6,2)

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_product_cones.cpp gains a mode sym. It computes each witness as \(\Phi_pP'\), with \(P'\) in the trivial or else the sign part, and prints \(\dim V_p\) by part 2 of the lemma. It prints a fingerprint of the normal form along \(L\), normalized by its first nonzero coefficient, and then evaluates the product cones as before.

Finite check (check:cube-product-cones-six-two, research/results/bmd-r73-six-two/). Over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\):

  • Validation at \((4,2)\). The symmetric mode reproduces the dense solve: the same fingerprints for \(P_1,P_2,P_3\), \(\dim V_p=1\) for each (all in the trivial part), and rank 2.
  • \(P_4\). \(\dim V_4=1\), with trivial part 1, sign 0, standard 0. It lies in \(J^8\), in agreement with the vertex-line theorem.
  • Top cones at \((6,2)\), \(m=25\). For \(P_3^2\) (\(\ell=16\), degree 8) the top cone is a multiple of \(U^4S^4\). For \(P_4P_2\) (\(\ell=18\), degree 10) it is a multiple of \(U^2S^2(U^4-S^4)(U^2-S^2)\): the coefficients are 197746 and \(-197746\) in the pattern \(1,-1,-1,1\). These are the cones of \(F_3^2\) and \(F_4F_2\) from the order theorem.
  • Rank. The \(2\times26\) matrix of cones has rank 2 at five random points \((\sigma,\tau)\). Eight coordinates of each solution have a zero cone.

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-six-two). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003:

  1. every local solution at \((d,\rho)=(6,2)\) (\(m=25\)) vanishes to order \(\ge\mu(6,2)=8\) at each double point;
  2. \(\ell_0(7,25)=B(6,2)=16\).

Proof. Part 1 follows the proof of thm:cube-order-half-four-two.

  • Lifting to \(\mathbb Q\). Over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(q=1000003\), \(\dim V_p=1\) for \(p=2,3,4\). Over \(\mathbb Q\) the dimension is at most that, and at least 1 by the boundary theorem. So a primitive integral generator reduces to the computed witness up to a scalar.
  • Normal forms. Over both fields the witnesses lie in \(J^{\psi(p)}\) by part 3 of the vertex-line theorem (\(p\le6\), with \(q\nmid p\)).
  • Independent cones. By the product cone formula the cones of the solutions of \(P_3^2\) and \(P_4P_2\) are computed by steps that commute with reduction. A nonzero minor over \(\mathbb F_q\) is therefore nonzero over \(\mathbb Q\), and the cones, of degrees \(\mu_A=8\) and \(\mu_B=10\), are independent over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\).
  • Squeeze. The solutions \(w_A\), \(w_B\) have multiplicities exactly 8 and 10, over \(\mathbb Q\) and over \(\mathbb F_q\). They are at least 8 and 10 because \(P_3^2\in J^8\) and \(P_4P_2\in J^{10}\) (vertex-line theorem part 3, product cone formula part 2). They are at most 8 and 10 because their degree-8 and degree-10 parts are nonzero, and a part nonzero modulo \(q\) is nonzero over \(\mathbb Q\). Part 1 of the squeeze lemma, with \(o_1=8\le o_2=10\), subtracts the larger multiplicity and gives \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge\pi-10\) for every local solution \(W\). Here \(\pi=\operatorname{mult}_PF_6\ge\psi(6)=18\) by the order theorem, since \(q\nmid6\). So \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge8\).
  • Other double points. They follow by the \(S_3\)-equivariance, as at \((4,2)\).

Part 2 is the sharp-pair threshold lemma. Hypothesis 1 is part 1. For hypothesis 2, the saved output of check:cube-line-splitting (research/results/bmd-r45-mixed-lifts/line-splitting-generic-through-P.txt, block \(d=6\), \(m=25\), \(\rho=2\), line through \((1,1,0)\) and \((7,3,11)\)) lists \(\dim(E_L)_l=0\) for \(l\le7\) and generators in degrees 8, 8. With the partition \((3,3)\), \(\beta(6,2)=2(\lceil3^2/2\rceil-1)=8\), so the datum is met, and \(B=\mu+\beta=16\). \(\square\)

In degree terms, along \(m=25\) the savings are at least 7 exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge16\).

General statement. lem:cube-witness-symmetry-reduction, for every \(p\) and every field of characteristic prime to 6.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: face divisibility, the product cone formula and its part 3 for odd \(e\) (here \(e=3\), \(\mu_A=8\), \(\mu_B=10\)), the squeeze lemma part 1, the order theorem's hypothesis for \(d=6\), the vertex-line theorem part 3, the sharp-pair threshold lemma, and the saved splitting block. Claim searches (symmetric witness, face-divided, standard representation) found no earlier version. Checks: the symmetric mode matches the dense solve in fingerprints, dimensions and rank at \((4,2)\). The top cones match the order theorem's branch product at \((6,2)\). A fresh-context referee checked the lemma (the dimension formula, the orbit representatives), the kernel (bases, sign table, rows, the \((12)\)-invariant count, the reconstruction), the outputs, the top cones and the splitting block. It found the lifting argument and the threshold application sound. Its corrections are made: the odd cases \((3,2)\), \((5,2)\) named and explained, the characteristics in the assessment, the exact multiplicities 8 and 10 in the squeeze step, the unsaved timings dropped, and \(\beta\) written from the partition.

Assessment. The second case of open statement 1 is proved, in characteristic 0 and 1000003 (the statement asks for every characteristic \(\ne2\)). It is the first case where the two product cones have different degrees. With symmetry the witnesses are small: \(P_4\) took seconds. So \(P_5\) and \(P_6\), for \((8,2)\) and \((10,2)\), are within reach, although the recorded splitting data stop at \(d=7\). The other cases of the computed splitting range are the odd cases \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\), and those with \(\rho\ge3\). They need solutions that are not products of boundary witnesses: at odd \(d\) the products fall short, as in the Question, and the squeeze entry found that products do not supply enough for most \(\rho\ge3\). That, and a general proof of the cone independence, are the open parts of this line.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: products are exhausted after (4,2) and (6,2); the next solutions must come from multiplication maps

Route review; products of boundary witnesses meet the squeeze only at (4,2) and (6,2) in the computed range; there they form a local basis. Cycle bmd-r74. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. Open statement 1: on \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)\ge B(d,\rho)\) for \(d\ge3\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\). The line proves it case by case through the sharp pair. The order half comes from the squeeze lemma with product solutions whose cones are computed by the product cone formula. The splitting half is a recorded finite datum. The sharp-pair threshold lemma combines them.

What the goal needs. Open statement 1 for every \((d,\rho)\) in every characteristic \(\ne2\). Case-by-case results reach at most the computed splitting range \(3\le d\le7\), and only in the certified characteristics.

Where the line stands. Since the last review:

  • Two-line peeling proved the vertex-line order for \(p\le6\) (vertex-line theorem).
  • Product cones proved the order half at \((4,2)\).
  • The sharp pair proved \(\ell_0(5,17)=6\) and, with symmetric face-divided witnesses, \(\ell_0(7,25)=16\) (threshold at (6,2)), in characteristic 0 and 1000003.

These are the first two cases of open statement 1.

Falsification attempt

At \((d,\rho)\) the product witnesses are \(\prod P_{p_i}\) over partitions of \(d\) into exactly \(\rho\) parts. The product of \(r\) boundary witnesses has savings \(d+1\) and \(m=4d+r-1\), so \(r=\rho\). Its solution has multiplicity \(o=\sum\psi(p_i)\), \(\psi(p)=\lfloor p^2/2\rfloor\). The squeeze needs \(\rho\) solutions with independent cones and \(\pi-(\text{sum of the }\rho-1\text{ largest }o)\ge\mu\), where \(\pi=\psi(d)\). Distinct partitions are therefore necessary. The claim under test is that products suffice across the computed range. research/tools/bmd_route_review_r74_tests.py checks this necessary condition for all 15 cases \(3\le d\le7\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\) (research/results/bmd-r74-route-review/tests.txt). It holds only at \((4,2)\) and \((6,2)\). Everywhere else it fails in one of two ways:

  • there are fewer than \(\rho\) partitions, as at \((3,2)\), \((4,3)\) and \((5,4)\);
  • the multiplicities are too high: at \((5,2)\) the products have 6 and 8 against \(\pi-\mu=6\), and at \((7,3)\) they have 8, 8, 10 against \(\pi-\mu=16\).

So the claim is falsified in 13 of 15 cases: the product route is exhausted in the computed range. Every further case needs solutions that are not products of boundary witnesses.

Assessment of this line

The mechanism is sound and now well understood where it applies. At \((4,2)\) and \((6,2)\) the product solutions are even a local basis of the solution module (Hilbert–Burch lead below). The case-by-case line cannot go further without a new supply of solutions. It also cannot reach every \((d,\rho)\) or every characteristic. What would help is structural: how the local solution module is generated. The multiplication-map lead below turns that into an induction whose base cases are the products already handled. The line's prospects depend on that induction. As a case list it is finished.

Outside leads

  • The Hilbert–Burch theorem (Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra, Theorem 20.15). A free submodule \(L\subseteq M\) of the same rank equals \(M\) exactly when its maximal minors have the same order as those of \(M\). The minors of \(M\) are \(F_d\) times a unit (Plücker bound). This targets the order half: product solutions whose cone minor is the cone of \(F_d\) are a local basis of \(M\), so every local solution is a combination of them. It would break if the minor had a higher order than \(\pi\). Test. Passed. At \((4,2)\) the cone minor \(2^{17}U^2S^2(U^4-S^4)\) is a multiple of the cone of \(F_4\). At \((6,2)\) the minor divided by \(U^4S^4\) is a multiple of \(U^2S^2(U^6-S^6)\) (test 3), so the minor is a multiple of \(U^6S^6(U^6-S^6)\), the cone of \(F_6\). In both cases the two product solutions generate \(M\) locally.
  • Mumford's theta basis for degree-\(\rho\) bundles (D. Mumford, On the equations defining abelian varieties, Invent. Math. 1, 1966; the Tate curve). By the residue duality, solutions at \(m\) are Laurent tails of \(\varphi\omega_0\) with \(\varphi\in L((m+1)p_0-dH_\infty)\), a bundle of degree \(m+1-4d=\rho\). So \(M\) is the module of sections of a degree-\(\rho\) bundle on the Tate family over \(F[[s,t]]\), and products of boundary solutions are products of degree-1 sections. Products of sections of \(L_1,\ldots,L_\rho\) give one section of \(\bigotimes L_i\) for each splitting, so they span at most as many dimensions as there are partitions. This targets the supply of non-product solutions: they are the degree-\(\rho\) theta functions that are not products. It would break if \(M\) were not the full section module. Test. Passed: the degree of the bundle is \(\rho=\operatorname{rank}M\) (the rank of the free local module), and the partition counts of test 1 explain every failure with too few products.
  • Mumford's multiplication theorem on elliptic curves (D. Mumford, Varieties defined by quadratic equations, 1970; for an elliptic curve, \(H^0(L)\otimes H^0(L')\to H^0(L\otimes L')\) is onto when \(\deg L\ge2\), \(\deg L'\ge3\)). Carried over the Tate family, surjectivity would make \(M(d,\rho)\) locally generated by products \(M(d_1,\rho_1)\cdot M(d_2,\rho_2)\) with \(\rho_1\ge2\), \(\rho_2\ge3\). A product's multiplicity is the sum of its factors' multiplicities, and a combination's is at least their minimum. So the order half would follow by induction from base cases \(\rho\le4\) with the min-plus recursion \(\mu(d,\rho)=\min[\mu(d_1,\rho_1)+\mu(d_2,\rho_2)]\). This targets open statement 1 in general. It would break at the degenerate fibre, where surjectivity can fail, and in the base cases. Test. Passed for the recursion: \(\mu\) is the \(\rho\)-fold min-plus convolution of \(\psi\) (route review of 25 September), hence associative over splittings \(\rho=\rho_1+\rho_2\). The surjectivity at the degenerate fibre was not tested.

Absurd bridges

  • The parity effect in superconducting islands (condensed-matter physics: Tuominen, Hergenrother, Tighe and Tinkham, PRL 69, 1992; Averin–Nazarov). There the energy to add electrons to an island alternates with the parity of the charge, because electrons pair. The translation: a part \(p\) is the charge of an island, \(\psi(p)\) its energy, and \(\mu(d,\rho)\) the ground-state energy of \(\rho\) islands sharing \(d\) charges. The increments of \(\psi\) come in pairs, \(0,2,2,4,4,6,6,8,8\), so the balanced split is degenerate with its neighbour exactly when the halves are even. The theorem there predicts that \((2e,2)\) is tight (\(2\mu=\pi\)) exactly for even \(e\), where both products have the ground-state energy. Test. Passed (test 4): tight for \(e=2,4\) and not for \(e=3,5\).
  • Forney's minimal bases (control theory: G. D. Forney, SIAM J. Control 13, 1975; Kailath, Linear Systems, §6.5). The minimal indices of a polynomial matrix sum to the degree of its maximal minors less the degree of their gcd. The translation: the restriction of the solution system to a line is a polynomial matrix in \((u_0,u_1)\), and its minimal indices are the generator degrees \(b_i\) of \(E_L\). A theorem there gives the sum of the splitting type, which is the record's degree identity. It also offers realization theory (state-space models of minimal McMillan degree) for the splitting half. The smallest test is the identity in every recorded block. Test. Passed (test 2): \(\sum b_i=d^2-1-\binom\rho2-\pi\) in all 14 blocks on the line through \((1,1,0)\) and \((7,3,11)\).

Next step

The highest-risk item is the supply of non-product solutions. Take the smallest case, \((3,2)\), which is tight with \(\mu=2\) and \(\pi=4\) and has the single product \(P_2P_1\). Compute the global solutions at \(m=13\) of excess \(3\) to about \(8\) (symmetric face-divided witnesses), their vertex-line orders, and their cones by part 1 of the product cone formula. If one has multiplicity 2 with a cone independent of \(P_2P_1\)'s, then the order half at \((3,2)\) holds, and with the recorded splitting datum so does \(\ell_0(4,13)=3\). Then ask whether such solutions are products in the sense of the multiplication-map lead, and test that lead's surjectivity at the degenerate fibre.

Process. One small script on saved data. The falsification test could have supported the product route and instead showed that it ends at \((6,2)\).

26 September 2026 — A non-product generator: the threshold at (3,2), ℓ₀(4,13) = 3, and a solution module that looks free

Working proof that ℓ₀(4,13) = 3 in characteristic 0 and 1000003, from a non-product solution certified exactly over Q; conjecture that the global solution module is free. Cycle bmd-r75. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review found products of boundary witnesses exhausted after \((4,2)\) and \((6,2)\). At \((3,2)\) (\(m=13\), \(\mu=2\), \(\pi=\psi(3)=4\), tight) the only product is \(P_2P_1\). Does some other global solution of multiplicity 2 have a tangent cone independent of that product's? If so, the squeeze gives the order half, and the recorded splitting datum gives the threshold. The test ends with such a solution certified over \(\mathbb Q\), or with the cone rank stuck at 1.

All solutions, not only products

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_solution_cones.cpp computes over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(q=1000003\), for each excess \(\ell\), the whole space \(V_\ell\) of witnesses at \((d,\rho)\). These have savings \(d+1\), \(k=\ell+m+1\), degree \(\le2k-d\), multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices and origin order \(\ge\ell\), in face-divided form \(\prod(x_i-1)^dP'\) (face divisibility). A witness is determined by its solution: two witnesses with the same jet below degree \(k\) differ by a polynomial of degree \(<2k\) with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at all eight vertices, which is zero by the multiplicity Schwartz–Zippel lemma. Conversely, by part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma every solution of excess \(\ell\) comes from a witness of degree \(\le2k-d\), and face divisibility puts every such witness in the kernel's form. So \(\dim V_\ell\) is the dimension of the solutions of excess \(\ell\). For each basis element the kernel checks that the jet lies in \(J^{\,j}+\mathfrak m_0^k\), that is, that the solution has multiplicity \(\ge j\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) (vertex-line lemma, part 1). It computes the degree-\(j\) parts of the solution by part 1 of the product cone formula, whose proof uses only the jet. It reports the rank at a random point \((\sigma,\tau)\) of all degree-\(j\) cones of excess \(\le\ell\). This is a lower bound for the rank over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\). The values below equal that rank: a value 1 comes from a single nonzero vector or from the \(y_i\)-multiples of it, and a value 2 is at most \(\rho\) once the order half holds (squeeze lemma, part 2).

Validation at \((4,2)\) (\(j=4\), \(\ell=6,7,8\)): \(\dim V_\ell=1,3,7\), and the cone rank at a random point is 1, 1, 2. It reaches 2 at \(\ell=8\), where \(P_3P_1\) enters, as before.

At \((3,2)\) (\(j=2\), \(\ell=3,\ldots,10\)):

  • \(\dim V_\ell=1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64\), that is \((\ell-2)^2\);
  • every jet lies in \(J^2+\mathfrak m_0^k\);
  • the cone rank at a random point is 1 at \(\ell=3\) (the product \(P_2P_1\)) and 2 from \(\ell=4\) on.

The space \(V_4\) has dimension 4. Three of its dimensions are the multiples \(x_i(x_i-1)P_2P_1\): multiplying a witness by \(L(x_i)=x_i^2-x_i\) raises the multiplicity at every vertex by one, and it corresponds to multiplying the solution by \(y_i\). Multiplying by \(y_1\) or \(y_2\), which are units at \((1{:}1{:}0)\), keeps the cone direction of \(P_2P_1\), and multiplying by \(y_3\), which vanishes there, gives a zero degree-2 part. Any element of \(V_4\) outside the span of the three multiples is a witness that is not a product of boundary witnesses, since \(P_2P_1\) is the only such product at \((3,2)\) (route review). Its cone is independent of \(P_2P_1\)'s: the multiples contribute only the direction of \(P_2P_1\) or zero, while the cumulative rank at \(\ell=4\) is 2.

Exact checks over \(\mathbb Q\) (research/tools/bmd_cube_witness_rank_q.cpp, FLINT's multimodular exact fmpz_mat_rref_mul). For \(\ell=3,4\) the integer systems have rank 2289 and 2901, so \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}V_3=1\) and \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}V_4=4\), the dimensions over \(\mathbb F_q\). Adding the rows that put the jet of \(P'\) in \(J^2+\mathfrak m_0^k\) leaves both ranks unchanged. Since \(\prod(x_i-1)^3\) is a unit at the origin, every rational witness of excess 3 or 4 has multiplicity \(\ge2\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\).

The threshold at (3,2)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-three-two). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003:

  1. every local solution at \((d,\rho)=(3,2)\) (\(m=13\)) vanishes to order \(\ge\mu(3,2)=2\) at each double point;
  2. \(\ell_0(4,13)=B(3,2)=3\).

Proof. Part 1, in four steps.

  • Lifting. Let \(\Lambda_\ell\subseteq\mathbb Z^{U}\) be the saturated lattice of integer solutions of the system of \(V_\ell\). Its rank is \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}V_\ell\), and its reduction modulo \(q\) is injective with image inside the kernel over \(\mathbb F_q\). The two dimensions are equal for \(\ell=3,4\), so the reduction is that whole kernel.
  • Cones over \(\mathbb Q\). For every rational witness in \(V_3\cup V_4\), the jet lies in \(J^2+\mathfrak m_0^k\) (exact check). So its solution has multiplicity \(\ge2\), and its degree-2 part is given by the product cone formula. The steps of that formula commute with reduction. So the degree-2 cone map on \(\Lambda_3\oplus\Lambda_4\) has rank over \(\mathbb Q(\sigma,\tau)\) at least its rank over \(\mathbb F_q(\sigma,\tau)\), which is at least the rank 2 at the evaluation point.
  • Two solutions. Hence there are two rational witnesses whose solutions \(w_1,w_2\) have nonzero, independent degree-2 cones. Their multiplicity at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) is therefore exactly 2.
  • Squeeze. Part 1 of the squeeze lemma gives \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge\pi-2\) for every local solution. Here \(\pi=\operatorname{mult}_PF_3\ge\psi(3)=4\) by the order theorem (characteristic 0, or \(q\nmid3\)). So \(\operatorname{mult}_PW\ge2\).

Over \(\mathbb F_q\) the same computation applies directly. The other double points follow by the \(S_3\)-equivariance of the system, as at \((4,2)\).

Part 2 is the sharp-pair threshold lemma with \(\beta=B-\mu=1\). The saved output of check:cube-line-splitting (research/results/bmd-r45-mixed-lifts/line-splitting-generic-through-P.txt, block \(d=3\), \(m=13\), \(\rho=2\), line through \((1,1,0)\) and \((7,3,11)\)) lists \(\dim(E_L)_0=0\) and \(\dim(E_L)_1=1\). \(\square\)

In degree terms, along \(m=13\) the savings are at least 4 exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge3\).

The solution module looks free

The dimensions \((\ell-2)^2=\binom{\ell-1}2+\binom{\ell-2}2\) are the Hilbert function of \(S(-3)\oplus S(-4)\), \(S=F[y_1,y_2,y_3]\). At \((4,2)\), \(1,3,7\) are those of \(S(-6)\oplus S(-8)\). In both cases the generator excesses sum to \(d^2-1-\binom\rho2\) (7 and 14). This is a consistency check. For a free module whose basis stays a basis of the restricted solutions on a general line \(L\) (that is, \(L\) avoids the common zeros of the basis's maximal minors), \(\sum b_i=\sum a_i\), and the degree identity with \(e_x(L)=0\) gives \(d^2-1-\binom\rho2\). The Hilbert-function fit covers only \(\ell\le10\) at \((3,2)\) and three values at \((4,2)\), all over \(\mathbb F_q\), and a Hilbert function does not by itself imply freeness.

Conjecture (conj:cube-solution-module-free). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic 0 and large characteristic, for \(1\le\rho\le d\), the graded module of global solutions at \(m=4d+\rho-1\) is free over \(F[y_1,y_2,y_3]\), on \(\rho\) generators of excesses \(a_1\le\cdots\le a_\rho\) with \(a_1=\ell_0(d+1,m)\) and \(\sum a_i=d^2-1-\binom\rho2\).

If it holds, and if local solutions are generated by global ones (the local module being the completed stalk of the sheaf of the global module), the local module \(M\) at a double point would have the global generators as a basis. So in tight cases the order half is a statement about \(\rho\) explicit polynomials: their multiplicities, and the independence of their cones. At \((3,2)\) and \((4,2)\) the generators are \(P_2P_1\) with the new witness, and \(P_2^2\) with \(P_3P_1\).

General statement. conj:cube-solution-module-free, for every \((d,\rho)\) with \(1\le\rho\le d\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (witnesses and solutions of excess \(\ell\)), face divisibility, the vertex-line lemma part 1, the product cone formula part 1 (only the jet enters), the squeeze lemma part 1, the order theorem's hypothesis at \(d=3\), the sharp-pair threshold lemma and the saved splitting block. Claim searches (non-product witness, free solution module, generator excesses) found no earlier version. Checks: the kernel reproduces \((4,2)\). Exact rational ranks confirm the modular dimensions and the jet condition. A fresh-context referee checked the kernels (degree bound, face exponent, reduced multiplicities, Hasse rows, jet and normal form, series), the injectivity argument, the lifting from \(\mathbb F_q\) to \(\mathbb Q\), the exact jet check, the multiples, the squeeze step and the splitting block. It found them correct. Its corrections are made: the title, the evaluated rank as a lower bound with its upper bounds, the threshold-ideal lemma for the converse direction, the precise sense of "not a product", the hypothesis and limits of the freeness rationale, the local-basis claim made conditional, and the assessment restricted to tight cases.

Assessment. The first case of open statement 1 with odd \(d\) is proved, through a solution that is not a product of boundary witnesses. The method applies to any single tight case (\(\rho\mu=\pi\)): compute all solutions of low excess, certify exactly over \(\mathbb Q\), take cones by the product cone formula, then squeeze and split. It succeeds when the cone rank reaches \(\rho\) at a computable excess, the dimensions over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb F_q\) agree, and a splitting datum exists over the same prime. The freeness conjecture would supply the structure that a general proof needs: \(\rho\) global generators per \((d,\rho)\), with known excess sum. The next question is what the generators are in general, and whether their cones are independent for a structural reason.
