26 September 2026 — Excess sums and bases: ℓ₀(2e+1, 8e+1) = 2e² − 2 for 2 ≤ e ≤ 7, and the solution module is free there

Working proofs: a basis criterion by excess sums, coprimality of consecutive boundary generators, and the thresholds and order half at (2e,2) (e ≤ 7, e ≤ 5) in characteristic 0 and 1000003. Cycle bmd-r76. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The Hilbert functions at \((3,2)\) and \((4,2)\) suggested that the global solution module is free (conjecture). The record proves one direction: if it is free, the generator excesses sum to \(N(d,\rho)=d^2-1-\binom\rho2\) (prop:cube-solution-degree-identity). Does the converse hold, so that \(\rho\) independent solutions with excess sum \(N\) form a basis? If so, which known solutions are bases, and what follows for the threshold? The test ends with a proved criterion and its instances, or with the step that fails.

The basis criterion

Setting. On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(1\le\rho\le d\), \(m=4d+\rho-1\) and \(S=F[y_1,y_2,y_3]\). A solution of excess \(a\) is a vector \(W\) in \(\ker A_m\) with \(W_c\in S\) homogeneous of degree \(a+m-c\). For \(4d\)-sets \(T\) of columns, \(M_T\) is the maximal minor of \(A_m\) on \(T\) and \(P_T=M_T/g_{3,d}\). As recorded in the degree identity, the \(P_T\) have no common factor, \(\deg g_{3,d}=6d^2\) and \(\deg M_{T}=\sum_{c\in T}c-(d-1)^2\). The recorded computation gives \(\tfrac{m(m+1)}2-\rho m-(d-1)^2-6d^2=N(d,\rho)\).

Lemma (lem:cube-excess-sum-basis). Let \(w_1,\ldots,w_\rho\) be solutions of excesses \(a_1,\ldots,a_\rho\), linearly independent over \(F(y)\).

  1. \(\sum_ia_i\ge N(d,\rho)\).
  2. If \(\sum_ia_i=N(d,\rho)\), then every solution is an \(S\)-combination of the \(w_i\). At every point \(y_0\) of \(\mathbb P^2\), every local solution (in the completed local ring) is a combination of the \(w_i\) with coefficients in that ring. So the solution module is free with basis \(w_1,\ldots,w_\rho\).
  3. In the case of part 2, every solution with nonzero top coordinate has excess \(\ge\min_ia_i\), so \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\ge\min_ia_i\).

Proof.

  • Minors. \(A_m\) has rank \(4d\) over \(F(y)\) (Plücker bound), so \(\ker A_m\) has dimension \(\rho\) over \(F(y)\) and the \(w_i\) are a basis of it. For any \(\rho\) kernel vectors, the \(\rho\times\rho\) minors on column sets \(S'\) are \(G_{S'}=h\,\varepsilon_{S'}M_{S'^c}\) with one \(h\in F(y)\) for all \(S'\), as in the Plücker bound.
  • Part 1. Write \(hg_{3,d}=a/b\) in lowest terms. Then \(G_{S'}=(a/b)\varepsilon_{S'}P_{S'^c}\) is a polynomial for every \(S'\), so \(b\) divides every \(P_T\), and \(b\) is a constant. So \(G_{S'}=H\varepsilon_{S'}P_{S'^c}\) with a homogeneous \(H\in S\), nonzero by independence. Degrees give \(\deg G_{S'}=\sum_ia_i+\rho m-\sum_{c\in S'}c\) and \(\deg P_{S'^c}=\sum_{c\notin S'}c-(d-1)^2-6d^2\). Hence \(\deg H=\sum_ia_i-N(d,\rho)\ge0\).
  • Part 2. If \(\sum a_i=N\), then \(H\) is a nonzero constant. Let \(W\) be a solution. Over \(F(y)\), \(W=\sum_ir_iw_i\), and by Cramer's rule \(r_i=G_{S'}(w_1,\ldots,W,\ldots,w_\rho)/G_{S'}(w)\) for any \(S'\) with \(P_{S'^c}\ne0\). The numerator is \(H_i\varepsilon_{S'}P_{S'^c}\) with \(H_i\in S\), by the argument of part 1 applied to that tuple, or zero. So \(r_i=H_i/H\in S\). Locally at \(y_0\), dehomogenize in a chart containing \(y_0\) and work in the completed local ring \(\hat{\mathcal O}_{y_0}\), a factorial domain. \(A_m\) keeps rank \(4d\) over its fraction field. The \(P_T\) have no common non-unit factor there. Since their global gcd is 1, their common zero set \(V(P_T:\text{all }T)\) is finite: a curve in it would be \(V(f)\) with \(f\) irreducible dividing every \(P_T\). So the \(P_T\) generate an \(\mathfrak m\)-primary or unit ideal of \(\hat{\mathcal O}_{y_0}\). A common non-unit factor \(f\) would give \(1=\dim\hat{\mathcal O}/(f)\le\dim\hat{\mathcal O}/(P_T)_T=0\). So \(hg_{3,d}\in\hat{\mathcal O}_{y_0}\) for the local tuple, and \(r_i\in\hat{\mathcal O}_{y_0}\).
  • Part 3. A solution \(W=\sum c_iw_i\) with homogeneous \(c_i\in S\) has excess \(a_i+\deg c_i\) for each \(i\) with \(c_i\ne0\). \(\square\)

Part 2 with the recorded direction shows that the solution module is free exactly when some \(\rho\) independent solutions have excess sum \(N(d,\rho)\).

Consecutive boundary generators are coprime

Lemma (lem:cube-boundary-generators-coprime). In characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(d,d'\ge1\) be coprime.

  1. Every common irreducible factor of \(F_d=\Delta_{3,d}/g_{3,d}\) and \(F_{d'}\) is a collision form \(y_i\) or \(y_i-y_j\).
  2. If \(\operatorname{mult}_PF_d=\lfloor d^2/2\rfloor\) at the double points (for \(d\le7\) in characteristic 0 and 1000003, check:cube-boundary-double-point-order-exact, under the hypothesis of the order theorem), then \(F_d\) has no collision factor, so \(\gcd(F_d,F_{d'})=1\).

Proof. Part 1. Pass to \(\bar F\). This changes neither the gcd nor the irreducible factors up to Galois conjugacy, and a collision form stays one. Let \(U\) be the set of points with distinct nonzero coordinates. At \(y\in U\), by residue duality with \(m=4d\), the solutions form the line of Laurent tails of \(\varphi\omega_0\), \(\varphi\in L((4d+1)p_0-dH_\infty)\), a divisor class of degree 1. The top coordinate vanishes exactly when \(\varphi\) has pole order \(\le4d\) at \(p_0\). That happens exactly when \(L(4dp_0-dH_\infty)\ne0\), which, for a divisor of degree 0 on the genus-1 curve \(\bar C_{4y}\), means \(d(H_\infty-4p_0)\sim0\), that is \(d\cdot c=0\) with \(c=[H_\infty-4p_0]\). The primitive boundary solution \(W^{(d)}\) spans this line wherever \(W^{(d)}(y)\ne0\), which fails only on a finite set \(Z_d\) (its coordinates have no common factor). So on \(U\setminus Z_d\), \(F_d(y)=W^{(d)}_{4d}(y)=0\) exactly when \(d\cdot c(y)=0\).

For \(d=1\), \(F_1\) has degree \(1-1=0\) and is nonzero, so \(c(y)\ne0\) on \(U\setminus Z_1\). A common factor of \(F_d\) and \(F_{d'}\) that is not a collision form defines a curve meeting \(U\setminus(Z_1\cup Z_d\cup Z_{d'})\) in infinitely many points. At each of them \(d\cdot c=d'\cdot c=0\), so \(c=0\), a contradiction.

Part 2. Permuting the coordinates permutes the rows of \(A\), so \(F_d\) is symmetric up to sign, and its multiplicity and branch divisibility at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) hold at \((1{:}0{:}1)\) and \((0{:}1{:}1)\) too. The same symmetry carries part 2 of the theorem below to all double points. Every collision line passes through a double point: \(y_3=0\) and \(y_1=y_2\) through \((1{:}1{:}0)\), and the others through \((1{:}0{:}1)\) and \((0{:}1{:}1)\) by symmetry. In the chart \(y_2=1\), \(y_1=1+t\), \(y_3=s\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\), the lines are \(t=0\) and \(s=0\). By the order theorem, \(F_d\) is divisible in \(F[[s,t]]\) by \(\prod_{m=1}^{d-1}(t^{2(d-m)}A^{2d}-s^{2m}C^{2m})\), of multiplicity \(\lfloor d^2/2\rfloor\), with \(A,C\) units. No factor is divisible by \(s\) or \(t\). If \(t\) or \(s\) divided \(F_d\), the multiplicity would exceed \(\lfloor d^2/2\rfloor\). \(\square\)

The thresholds at (2e,2)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-even-two). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003:

  1. for \(2\le e\le7\), the solutions \(w_A\), \(w_B\) of the products \(P_e^2\) and \(P_{e+1}P_{e-1}\) form a basis of the global solution module at \((d,\rho)=(2e,2)\), \(m=8e+1\), and of every local solution module. So the module is free (conj:cube-solution-module-free holds there), and \(\ell_0(2e+1,8e+1)=B(2e,2)=2e^2-2\);
  2. for \(2\le e\le5\), every local solution at \((2e,2)\) vanishes to order \(\ge\mu(2e,2)=2\psi(e)\) at each double point.

Proof. Part 1 has four steps.

  • Excess sum. The products are witnesses at \(m=8e+1\) with origin orders \(a_A=2(e^2-1)\) and \(a_B=((e+1)^2-1)+((e-1)^2-1)=2e^2\) (vertex-line entry). Their sum is \(4e^2-2=N(2e,2)\).
  • Independence. Their top coordinates are \(\pm F_e^2\) and \(\pm F_{e+1}F_{e-1}\), the lowest parts of the products. Suppose \(w_A=r\,w_B\) with \(r=a/b\in F(y)\) in lowest terms. Then \(a\) divides every coordinate of \(w_A\), and \(v=w_A/a=w_B/b\) is a solution with top coordinate \(v_m\ne0\), dividing both \(F_e^2\) and \(F_{e+1}F_{e-1}\). By the coprimality lemma, with \(e\le7\) giving exactness for \(F_e\) and \(e,e\pm1\) coprime, this gcd is 1. So \(v\) has excess 0 and a nonzero top coordinate, against \(\ell_0\ge2\) for \(\rho\le d-1\) (order-zero theorem). So \(w_A,w_B\) are independent.
  • Basis. By the basis criterion, \(w_A,w_B\) are a basis, globally and locally.
  • Threshold. Part 3 of the criterion gives \(\ell_0\ge\min(a_A,a_B)=2e^2-2\), and the product bound gives \(\le B(2e,2)=2(e^2-1)\). Here the balanced partition of \(2e\) into 2 parts is \((e,e)\).

Part 2. Every local solution is \(c_Aw_A+c_Bw_B\) with local coefficients, so its multiplicity at a double point is at least \(\min(\operatorname{mult}w_A,\operatorname{mult}w_B)\). By the vertex-line theorem (\(p\le6\), which needs \(e\le5\)) and part 2 of the vertex-line lemma, these are \(\ge2\psi(e)\) and \(\ge\psi(e+1)+\psi(e-1)\ge2\psi(e)\). \(\square\)

So open statement 1 holds at \((2e,2)\) for \(2\le e\le7\), that is \(d=4,6,\ldots,14\), in characteristic 0 and 1000003. The only restriction comes from the recorded exactness of \(\operatorname{mult}F_e\). At \((4,2)\) and \((6,2)\) this reproves the earlier thresholds without their cone certificates and without the splitting data. It relies instead on the recorded exactness check of \(\operatorname{mult}F_e\). At \((8,2)\), \((10,2)\), \((12,2)\) and \((14,2)\) the thresholds are new. The criterion also makes the module free at \((3,2)\). There the \((3,2)\) entry gives rational solutions of excesses 3 and 4, with \(3+4=7=N(3,2)\), whose degree-2 cones at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) are independent over \(F(\sigma,\tau)\). Cone independence implies independence over \(F(y)\): if \(bw'=aw\) with polynomials \(a,b\), then the lowest forms give \(\operatorname{cone}(b)\operatorname{cone}(w')=\operatorname{cone}(a)\operatorname{cone}(w)\), and the cones would be dependent.

General statement. lem:cube-excess-sum-basis, for every \((d,\rho)\), and lem:cube-boundary-generators-coprime, for all coprime \(d,d'\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the degree identity (coprime \(P_T\), degrees of \(M_T\) and \(g\), the constant \(N\)), the Plücker bound, residue duality, the order theorem's divisibility at the double points, the exactness check, the order-zero theorem, the product bound, the vertex-line theorem and lemma, and prop:cube-solution-degree-identity (the forward direction). Claim searches (excess sum, basis, free solution module, Cramer, minors) found only the forward direction and the freeness conjecture. A fresh-context referee checked every step: the constant \(N\), the degree count, the Cramer step, residue duality at \(\rho=1\), the \(F_1\) and Bezout steps, the collision lines through the double points, the branch multiplicity, the independence argument and the numbers \(m=8e+1\), \(a_A,a_B\), \(N(2e,2)\). It found no gap in the proof. Its corrections are made: the local coprimality argued for the whole family of \(P_T\), the passage to \(\bar F\), the symmetry of \(F_d\) for the other double points, the independence of the \((3,2)\) solutions justified through their cones, and the assessment qualified by the exactness check.

Assessment. The case-by-case line has turned into a structural one. A solution module is free exactly when some \(\rho\) independent solutions have the right excess sum, and then the threshold is the least generator excess, with no splitting datum needed. For \(\rho=2\) and even \(d\), the products are such a basis because consecutive boundary generators are coprime. The elliptic curve's division loci show that any common factor is a collision form, and the recorded exactness check excludes collision factors for \(e\le7\). Beyond \(e\le7\), only the collision factors of \(F_e\) are missing for the threshold. The order half also needs the vertex-line theorem beyond \(p\le6\). Odd \(d\) and \(\rho\ge3\) need other generators, as at \((3,2)\). The criterion now says what to look for: \(\rho\) independent solutions with excess sum \(N\).

26 September 2026 — Boundary generators have no collision factor: ℓ₀(2e+1, 8e+1) = 2e² − 2 for every e ≥ 2 in every characteristic ≠ 2

Working proof that F_d has no collision factor for every d; with the basis criterion it proves open statement 1 at (2e,2) for all e ≥ 2 over every field of characteristic ≠ 2. Cycle bmd-r77. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The even-case theorem proves \(\ell_0=B\) at \((2e,2)\) for \(e\le7\). Its one restriction is that \(F_e\) has no collision factor \(y_i\) or \(y_i-y_j\), known only through the recorded exactness check for \(e\le7\). Does \(F_d\) vanish identically on a collision line for some \(d\)? The test ends with a proof for every \(d\), or with a collision line that divides some \(F_d\).

No collision factor

Lemma (lem:cube-boundary-generator-collision-free). Over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), for every \(d\ge1\), the boundary generator \(F_d=\Delta_{3,d}/g_{3,d}\) is divisible by no collision form \(y_i\) or \(y_i-y_j\).

Proof.

  1. Reduction to a limit space. By symmetry, take the divisor \(y_1=0\). For the divisors \(y_i=y_j\), see step 4. Let \(W\) be the primitive boundary solution (\(m=4d\)), so \(F_d=W_{4d}\). Its coordinates have no common factor, so \(y_1\) does not divide all of them. Take the arc \(\gamma=(\varepsilon,y_2,y_3)\) at the generic point of \(y_1=0\), over \(F'=F(y_2,y_3)\). Then \(W(\gamma)\) reduces modulo \(\varepsilon\) to \(W|_{y_1=0}\ne0\). As in the proof of the boundary coordinate theorem, \(W(\gamma)\) kills \(\tau_{4d}(\Lambda_\gamma)\), so \(W|_{y_1=0}\) kills \(\tau_{4d}(S)\) for the limit space \(S\). By the flat-limit order bound \(\tau_{4d}\) is injective on \(S\), and \(\dim S=4d\). So \(W|_{y_1=0}\) spans the annihilator of the hyperplane \(\tau_{4d}(S)\). Its top coordinate \(F_d|_{y_1=0}\) vanishes exactly when \(S\) contains an element of \(T\)-order exactly \(4d\).
  2. The limit space. By the collision limit lemma, \(S=U=\operatorname{span}_{F'}\{T^Qz_2^{r_2}z_3^{r_3}:Q+r_2+r_3\le d\}\), with \(z_i=r_0(y_iT)=(1-w_i)/2\) and \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\). Changing between \(z_i\) and \(w_i\) is triangular in \(|r|\). So \(U\) is the set of \(f=A+Bw_2+Cw_3+Dw_2w_3\) with \(A,B,C,D\in F'[T]\), \(\deg A\le d\), \(\deg B,\deg C\le d-1\) and \(\deg D\le d-2\). This representation is unique, since \(1,w_2,w_3,w_2w_3\) is a basis over \(F'(T)\) (Kummer theory, as in that lemma).
  3. No element of order \(4d\).
    • The functions \(w_2,w_3\) live on the conic \(\Gamma:\ y_3(w_2^2-1)=y_2(w_3^2-1)\), which is smooth and rational since \(y_2,y_3\) are nonzero and distinct. It has \(p_0=(1,1)\) at \(T=0\), where \(T\) is a local parameter (the zeros of \(T\) are the four points \(w_2,w_3=\pm1\)), and two points \(\infty_1,\infty_2\) at infinity. These are conjugate over \(F'(\sqrt{y_2/y_3})\), but the divisor \(\infty_1+\infty_2\) is \(F'\)-rational, so the dimension counts below hold over \(F'\). \(T\) has a double pole at each point at infinity, and \(w_i\) a simple pole. So \(U\subseteq L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2))\), a space of dimension \(4d+1\) on \(\Gamma\cong\mathbb P^1\). Since \(\dim U=(d+1)+d+d+(d-1)=4d\), \(U\) is a hyperplane in it. It is exactly the hyperplane cut out by the \(w_2w_3T^{d-1}\) coefficient, which is the only coefficient of an element of \(L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2))\) allowed by the pole orders that \(U\) forbids.
    • Its elements of order \(\ge4d\) at \(p_0\) form \(L(2d(\infty_1+\infty_2)-4dp_0)\), of dimension 1. This space is spanned by \(\varphi^{2d}\), where \(\varphi=y_3(w_2-1)-y_2(w_3-1)\) is the tangent line at \(p_0\). The line \(\varphi=0\) meets the line at infinity at the point with \(w_2/w_3=y_2/y_3\), which is not on \(\Gamma\) since \(y_3(y_2/y_3)^2\ne y_2\) for \(y_2\ne y_3\). So \(\operatorname{div}\varphi=2p_0-\infty_1-\infty_2\).
    • Give \(T\) weight 2 and \(w_i\) weight 1. The reduction \(w_i^2\to1+4y_iT\) never raises weight. So the part of weight \(2d\) of the reduced \(\varphi^{2d}\) is the reduction of \((y_3w_2-y_2w_3)^{2d}\) under the homogeneous rule \(w_i^2\to4y_iT\), and a coefficient \(D\) of degree \(d-1\) can come only from it. The part of \(\varphi^2\) of weight 2 is \(y_3^2w_2^2+y_2^2w_3^2-2y_2y_3w_2w_3\), whose leading part is \(2y_2y_3\bigl(aT-w_2w_3\bigr)\) with \(a=2(y_2+y_3)\), using \(w_i^2=1+4y_iT\). So the part of \(\varphi^{2d}\) of weight \(2d\) is \((2y_2y_3)^d(aT-w_2w_3)^d\).
    • Reduce \((w_2w_3)^2=(1+4y_2T)(1+4y_3T)\), whose leading term is \(b^2T^2\) with \(b^2=16y_2y_3\). Then the coefficient of \(w_2w_3T^{d-1}\) in \(\varphi^{2d}\) is \((2y_2y_3)^d\sum_{i\text{ odd}}\binom di a^{d-i}(-1)^ib^{i-1}=(2y_2y_3)^d\,\dfrac{(a-b)^d-(a+b)^d}{2b}\). Only the part of weight \(2d\) can contribute to that monomial.
    • Here \(a\pm b=2(\sqrt{y_2}\pm\sqrt{y_3})^2\). So the coefficient vanishes exactly when \(\zeta^{2d}=1\), with \(\zeta=(\sqrt{y_2}-\sqrt{y_3})/(\sqrt{y_2}+\sqrt{y_3})\). Now \(y_2/y_3=((1+\zeta)/(1-\zeta))^2\) is transcendental over the prime field, so \(\zeta\) is not a root of unity. So \(\deg D=d-1\) for \(\varphi^{2d}\), and \(\varphi^{2d}\notin U\).
    • Hence \(U\) has no element of order \(\ge4d\) at \(p_0\), and \(F_d|_{y_1=0}\ne0\). Examples: \(d=1\) gives \(D=-2y_2y_3\), and \(d=2\) gives a nonzero multiple of \(y_2+y_3\).
  4. The divisors \(y_i=y_j\). Take \(y_1=y_j\); the divisor \(y_2=y_3\) follows from it by the permutation symmetry of \(F_d\) up to sign. Step 1 applies unchanged to the arc \((y_j+\varepsilon,y_2,y_3)\): \(W|_{y_1=y_j}\ne0\), \(\dim S=4d\), and \(\tau_{4d}\) is injective on \(S\). In the collision limit lemma's notation \(a=4y\), \(w_i=(1+a_iT)^{1/2}\). The Möbius transport identifies \(S\) with the space \(\tilde U\) built from \(\tilde a=(a_1-a_j,-a_j,a_k-a_j)\), whose last two entries play the roles of \(4y_2,4y_3\) in step 3: they are algebraically independent, nonzero and distinct. The identification is the substitution \(\tilde T=T/(1+a_jT)\) followed by division by the unit \(\tilde w_j^{\,d}\), \(\tilde w_j=(1-a_j\tilde T)^{1/2}\), and both preserve the \(T\)-order at \(p_0\). Step 3 applied to \(\tilde U\) shows there is no element of order \(4d\) there either. \(\square\)

With the coprimality lemma, part 1, this gives \(\gcd(F_d,F_{d'})=1\) for all coprime \(d,d'\), in every characteristic \(\ne2\). The exactness check is no longer needed.

The thresholds at (2e,2) for every e

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-even-two-all). Over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\) and for every \(e\ge2\), the solutions of \(P_e^2\) and \(P_{e+1}P_{e-1}\) form a basis of the global and of every local solution module at \((d,\rho)=(2e,2)\), \(m=8e+1\). So the module is free, and \(\ell_0(2e+1,8e+1)=B(2e,2)=2e^2-2\).

Proof. This is the proof of part 1 of the even-case theorem. There, exactness entered only to exclude collision factors of \(F_e\), and the lemma above does so for every \(e\). The remaining ingredients are all recorded in every characteristic \(\ne2\):

  • the basis criterion;
  • part 1 of the coprimality lemma, through residue duality;
  • the order-zero theorem, over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\);
  • the product bound, in characteristic \(\ne2\);
  • the boundary witnesses and \(F_d\) of degree \(d^2-1\), from the boundary threshold theorem, over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\);
  • the top coordinates \(\pm F_e^2\), \(\pm F_{e+1}F_{e-1}\) of the products, which are their lowest parts.

\(\square\)

So open statement 1 holds for \(\rho=2\) and every even \(d\ge4\), over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). In degree terms, along \(m=k-\ell-1=8e+1\) the savings are at least \(2e+1\) exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge2e^2-2\). The order half at \((2e,2)\) still needs the vertex-line theorem, so it remains proved for \(e\le5\) under the order theorem's hypothesis.

General statement. lem:cube-boundary-generator-collision-free and thm:cube-threshold-even-two-all, for every \(d\), \(e\) and characteristic \(\ne2\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the collision limit lemma (\(S=U^{(2)}_d\) at the generic point of \(y_1=0\), the Kummer basis, the Möbius transport for \(y_1=y_j\)), the boundary coordinate theorem's limit argument, the flat-limit bound, the coprimality lemma and the even-case theorem. Claim searches (collision factor, boundary generator, restriction to a collision line) found only the coprimality lemma, whose part 2 this replaces. A fresh-context referee found no mathematical gap and ran three symbolic checks. For \(d\le5\), reducing \(\varphi^{2d}\) gives coefficient degrees \((d,d-1,d-1,d-1)\) with the stated \(w_2w_3T^{d-1}\) coefficient (at \(d=3\): \(-32y_2^3y_3^3(y_2+3y_3)(3y_2+y_3)\)). On the branch \(w_i=\sqrt{1+4y_iT}\), \(\varphi^{2d}\) vanishes to order exactly \(4d\), with \(T^{4d}\) coefficient \((2y_2y_3)^{2d}(y_2-y_3)^{2d}\). A conic-free check: the \(4d\times4d\) matrix of the first \(4d\) coefficients of the basis of \(U\) has a nonzero determinant for \(d\le3\), whose factors match the coefficient formula. Its corrections are made: the transported coordinates and step 1 along \(y_1=y_j\) stated, the weight argument justified, the conic's divisor, rationality and hyperplane made explicit, the characteristic scope of every ingredient cited, and the assessment's wording.

Assessment. The first infinite family of open statement 1 is proved, in every characteristic \(\ne2\): \(\rho=2\), even \(d\). The mechanism is structural throughout. Products of boundary witnesses have the right excess sum. Consecutive boundary generators are coprime, because their zero loci are division loci of one point on an elliptic curve. None of them contains a collision line, because the only obstruction there is \(\zeta^{2d}=1\), and \(\zeta\) is not a root of unity since \(y_2/y_3\) is transcendental. Odd \(d\) and \(\rho\ge3\) need other generators. The basis criterion says what they must satisfy.

26 September 2026 — Odd d at ρ = 2: an invariant generator of excess B + 1, and ℓ₀(6,21) = 11

Working proof that ℓ₀(6,21) = B(5,2) = 11 in characteristic 0 and 1000003, from an S₃-invariant solution of excess 12. Cycle bmd-r78. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. Open statement 1 at \(\rho=2\) is proved for every even \(d\) (theorem). For odd \(d=2e+1\ge5\) the products \(P_{e+1}P_e\) and \(P_{e+2}P_{e-1}\) have excesses \(B\) and \(B+4\). At \(d=3\) only the first exists. Their sum \(2B+4\) exceeds \(N=d^2-2=2B+1\) by 3, so by the recorded degree identity (prop:cube-solution-degree-identity: the generators of a free module have excess sum \(N\)) they are not a basis. At \((3,2)\) a generator of excess \(B+1=4\) closed the gap (theorem). Does the same happen at \((5,2)\)? What is the generator's symmetry? The test ends with the threshold at \((5,2)\), or with no second generator of excess 12.

Solutions by character

The threshold at (5,2)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-five-two). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003, the solution module at \((d,\rho)=(5,2)\), \(m=21\), is free on the solution \(w\) of \(P_3P_2\) (excess 11) and an \(S_3\)-invariant solution \(v\) of excess 12. Hence \(\ell_0(6,21)=B(5,2)=11\).

Proof. Let \(q=1000003\).

  • Lifting. Let \(\Lambda\) be the saturated lattice of integer solutions of the trivial-part system at excess 12. The exact rank gives it rank 2, equal to the dimension over \(\mathbb F_q\). So its reduction is the whole trivial kernel over \(\mathbb F_q\). That kernel contains the multiple \((y_1+y_2+y_3)\bar w\), whose cone is \(2\) times that of \(\bar w\) since \(y_1+y_2+y_3=2\) at \((1{:}1{:}0)\). It also contains an element \(\bar v\) whose degree-6 cone is independent of \(\bar w\)'s, since the rank rises to 2 at excess 12. Lift \(\bar v\) to \(v\in\Lambda\). The map from witness to solution is defined over \(\mathbb Z_{(q)}\), since \(r_0\) has integer coefficients and \(L'(0)=-1\) is a unit, as in the \((4,2)\) order-half proof. So solutions of integral witnesses reduce to the solutions of the reduced witnesses. Take the rational product solution \(w\) primitive. It reduces to a nonzero multiple of \(\bar w\), because the trivial part at excess 11 is one-dimensional over \(\mathbb F_q\).
  • Independence over \(\mathbb Q(y)\). Suppose \(bv=aw\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z[y]\) coprime and the pair primitive. Reducing modulo \(q\) gives \(\bar b\bar v=\bar a\bar w\) with \((\bar a,\bar b)\ne(0,0)\). Then \(\bar b\ne0\), since otherwise \(\bar a\bar w=0\) with \(\bar w\ne0\). And \(\bar a\ne0\), since otherwise \(\bar v=0\). The jets of \(\bar v,\bar w\) lie in \(J^6+\mathfrak m_0^k\), and their degree-6 parts are nonzero, so these are their lowest forms at \((1{:}1{:}0)\). Taking lowest forms, \(\operatorname{cone}(\bar b)\operatorname{cone}(\bar v)=\operatorname{cone}(\bar a)\operatorname{cone}(\bar w)\), which contradicts the independence of the cones. The same argument, without reduction, works over \(\mathbb F_q\).
  • Basis. The excesses sum to \(11+12=23=5^2-1-\binom22=N(5,2)\). By the basis criterion, \(w,v\) are a basis globally and locally, and \(\ell_0\ge11\). The product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B(5,2)=8+3=11\). \(\square\)

In degree terms, along \(m=21\) the savings are at least 6 exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge11\). No splitting datum is used. The order half at \((5,2)\) is not needed for the threshold, and it is not proved.

The odd pattern

Conjecture (conj:cube-odd-invariant-generator). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), for odd \(d=2e+1\ge3\), the solution module at \((d,2)\) is free on the solution of \(P_{e+1}P_e\) (excess \(B=2e^2+2e-1\)) and an \(S_3\)-invariant solution of excess \(B+1=(d^2-1)/2\). Hence \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+1)=B(d,2)\) for every odd \(d\).

By the basis criterion it suffices to find, for each odd \(d\), one solution of excess \(B+1\) independent of the product's over \(F(y)\). The multiples \(y_iw\) never are. For \(d\ge5\), if the conjecture holds, the solution \(w_{B+4}\) of \(P_{e+2}P_{e-1}\) (excess \(B+4\)) is \(c_1w+c_2v\) with \(\deg c_1=4\) and \(\deg c_2=3\). If moreover \(w_{B+4}\) is independent of \(w\) over \(F(y)\), which is not yet checked, then \(c_2\ne0\), and the missing generator is \((w_{B+4}-c_1w)/c_2\). If that cubic can be identified, the construction becomes explicit.

General statement. conj:cube-odd-invariant-generator, for every odd \(d\ge3\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the basis criterion, the symmetry reduction, the product cone formula part 1, the product bound, and the \((3,2)\) proof, whose lifting argument this one simplifies. The simplification is that independence over \(\mathbb Q(y)\) follows from independence modulo \(q\), so only the dimension of the space holding the new generator must be matched over \(\mathbb Q\). Claim searches (invariant generator, odd degree, second generator) found only the \((3,2)\) entry and the freeness conjecture. The sym mode reproduces the recorded \((3,2)\) data. A fresh-context referee checked the sym-mode kernels (orbit sums, sign table, vertex representatives, reconstruction, rational row count), the lifting and independence argument, and the numbers \(B,B+1,N,\deg c_2\). It found no gap. Its corrections are made: the product placed in the trivial part by its character, the solution map over \(\mathbb Z_{(q)}\) with \(w\) primitive, \(\bar a\ne0\), the forward degree identity cited for "not a basis", the two-product statements restricted to \(d\ge5\), the independence of \(w_{B+4}\) stated as a hypothesis, and the status line shortened.

Assessment. Two odd cases now have the same structure: the product of the two middle boundary witnesses, plus one invariant generator of excess \(B+1\). A general proof for odd \(d\) needs only that generator. The relation \(P_{e+2}P_{e-1}=c_1w+c_2v\) with a cubic \(c_2\) is the most concrete handle on it.

26 September 2026 — Route review of the cube: ρ = 2 is reduced to one odd generator, and (4,3) looks free on generators 3, 4, 5

Route review; the freeness conjecture survives its first ρ = 3 test, whose Hilbert function is that of generators of excesses 3, 4, 5 with sum N. Cycle bmd-r79. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

The line's general claim. Open statement 1: on \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)\ge B(d,\rho)\) for \(d\ge3\), \(2\le\rho\le d-1\). The current route goes through the solution module. By the basis criterion, \(\rho\) solutions independent over \(F(y)\) with excess sum \(N=d^2-1-\binom\rho2\) are a basis, and then \(\ell_0\) is their least excess.

What the goal needs. For every \((d,\rho)\) in the range, such a basis with least excess \(B(d,\rho)\), in every characteristic \(\ne2\).

Where the line stands. Since the last review:

  • \((3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) were proved by an \(S_3\)-invariant non-product generator of excess \(B+1\), in characteristic 0 and 1000003 (theorem).
  • The basis criterion and coprime boundary generators proved \(\rho=2\) for every even \(d\), in every characteristic \(\ne2\) (theorem).
  • The odd case is conjectured (odd invariant generator).
  • Nothing is known yet for \(\rho\ge3\).

Falsification attempt

The freeness conjecture predicts, at every \((d,\rho)\), \(\rho\) generators with least excess \(B\) and excess sum \(N\). The first case with \(\rho=3\) is \((4,3)\): \(B=3\) (partition \((2)\) of 2), and \(N=16-1-3=12\). A free module \(\bigoplus S(-a_i)\) has Hilbert series \(\sum t^{a_i}/(1-t)^3\), so \((1-t)^3H(t)\) must be a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, \(\rho\) terms, least exponent \(B\) and exponent sum \(N\). Any failure refutes the conjecture at \((4,3)\).

The test computes the dimensions of all solution spaces at \((4,3)\), \(m=18\), for excess 3 to 9 (research/tools/bmd_cube_solution_cones.cpp, dense mode, over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), 169 s; research/results/bmd-r79-route-review/solution-spaces-four-three.txt). They are 1, 4, 10, 19, 31, 46, 64. Their third differences are 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. So \((1-t)^3H(t)=t^3+t^4+t^5\) through excess 9: three generators, at excesses 3, 4, 5, with sum \(12=N\), and least \(3=B\). The prediction survives.

The degree-2 cone rank at \((1{:}1{:}0)\) stays at 2. The third generator therefore has a larger multiplicity there, or a dependent cone. So its independence over \(F(y)\) needs another test: the rank of the solution vectors evaluated at a random point.

Assessment of this line

The structural route has been productive. In four cycles it gave an infinite family, \(\rho=2\) for every even \(d\), in every characteristic \(\ne2\), and two odd cases. Each case it touches reduces to exhibiting generators: one invariant generator per odd \(d\) at \(\rho=2\), and \(\rho-1\) new generators at \(\rho\ge3\). The \((4,3)\) data fit freeness exactly. The weak point is that the generators beyond products have no construction yet. Computation certifies them one case at a time, and a general proof needs their origin: theta functions of higher level, or a determinantal formula. Prospects for the whole of open statement 1 therefore rest on finding that construction. The case-by-case certificates now cost seconds to minutes, so they can supply data for guessing it.

Outside leads

  • Horrocks' splitting criterion (G. Horrocks, Proc. LMS 1964; Okonek–Schneider–Spindler, Vector Bundles on Complex Projective Spaces, Thm. I.2.3.1). A vector bundle on \(\mathbb P^2\) splits exactly when \(H^1(\tilde E(t))=0\) for all \(t\). The solution sheaf \(\tilde E\) is a kernel of a map of split bundles, so \(H^1_*(\tilde E)\) is a cokernel of global sections. That would give freeness for every \((d,\rho)\). This targets the freeness conjecture, hence open statement 1 once the least generator excess is known. It would break if the cokernel of \(A_m\) has \(H^0\) not generated by global data. Test. Passed at the level of Hilbert functions: \((4,3)\) matches \(\mathcal O(-3)\oplus\mathcal O(-4)\oplus\mathcal O(-5)\) through excess 9, a necessary condition for splitting. The vanishing of \(H^1_*\) was not tested.
  • Semistability of syzygy bundles (H. Brenner, Looking out for stable syzygy bundles, Adv. Math. 219, 2008). Syzygy bundles of general forms are semistable, and a split bundle \(\mathcal O(-a)\oplus\mathcal O(-b)\) with \(a\ne b\) is not. This would predict non-split solution modules. Test. Falsified as a predictor. At \((3,2)\) the module is proved to split as \(\mathcal O(-3)\oplus\mathcal O(-4)\), so the constraint matrices of the cube are far from general. The elliptic family forces the splitting, and a proof must use that structure.
  • Theta functions of level 2 (D. Mumford, Tata Lectures on Theta I, §I.9–I.10, the addition formula). By residue duality the solutions at \(\rho=2\) are sections of one bundle of degree 2 over the family. On each smooth fibre every section is a product of degree-1 sections, but the boundary witnesses supply only the degree-1 bundles \(L_p\). The odd generator should be the second theta function of the degree-2 bundle, whose zeros are not two boundary points, written by the addition formula. It targets conj:cube-odd-invariant-generator. It would break if the family's theta functions do not extend over the collision locus as polynomials. Test. Not run: it needs the addition formula over the Tate family \(F[[s,t]]\), which is not a cheap check.

Absurd bridges

  • Harmonic-oscillator spectroscopy (quantum mechanics). The level degeneracies of the three-dimensional isotropic oscillator are \(\binom{n+2}2\), the Hilbert function of \(S=F[y_1,y_2,y_3]\). The translation: a free solution module is the Fock space of \(\rho\) independent oscillators with ground energies \(a_i\), and the measured spectrum \(H(t)\) determines them by \((1-t)^3H(t)\). A theorem there, the uniqueness of that inversion, reads the generator excesses off the dimensions without knowing the generators. Test. Passed: the \((4,3)\) spectrum inverts to ground energies 3, 4, 5, nonnegative integers with multiplicity one each.
  • The Aufbau principle (chemistry: electrons fill the lowest free levels). The translation: after the least generator \(B\), the other generators occupy the next excesses one by one, subject to the sum \(N\). It predicts \((3,4,5)\) at \((4,3)\) and \((B,B+1)\) for odd \(d\) at \(\rho=2\). Test. Falsified as a universal rule, passed where it applies. It holds at \((4,3)\) and at \((3,2)\), \((5,2)\). It fails for even \(d\) at \(\rho=2\), where the generators \(2e^2-2\) and \(2e^2\) differ by 2, like a pairing gap.

Next step

The highest-risk item is still open statement 1 beyond \(\rho=2\) and odd \(d\).

  1. At \((4,3)\), certify three solutions of excesses 3, 4, 5 independent over \(F(y)\). Evaluate the solution vectors at a random point \(y_0\): the coordinates are the coefficients of \(\tilde w(ty_0)\), a one-variable series. Match the dimensions exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). The basis criterion then gives \(\ell_0(5,18)=3=B(4,3)\).
  2. Ask whether the family \(\rho=d-1\), where \(B=3\) for every \(d\), has a uniform basis.
  3. Pursue the theta lead for the odd generator.

Process. One computation, 169 s. The falsification test could have refuted the freeness conjecture, and it passed.

26 September 2026 — The first case with ρ = 3: ℓ₀(5,18) = 3, on generators of excesses 3, 4, 5

Working proof that ℓ₀(5,18) = B(4,3) = 3 in characteristic 0 and 1000003, by a basis certified at a random point. Cycle bmd-r80. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The route review found the Hilbert function of \(\mathcal O(-3)\oplus\mathcal O(-4)\oplus\mathcal O(-5)\) at \((4,3)\). Its degree-2 cones at the double point reach only rank 2, so they cannot show that three solutions are independent. Can independence over \(F(y)\) be certified directly, and does the basis criterion then give the threshold? The test ends with a certified basis, or with a value rank below 3.

Values at a random point

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_solution_cones.cpp gains a mode val. It evaluates every solution of excess \(\ell\) at a random point \(y_0\in\mathbb F_q^3\). The coordinates \(W_c(y_0)\) are the coefficients of \(t^{\ell+m-c}\) in the one-variable series \(\tilde w(ty_0)=P(r_0(ty_0))/\prod_iL'(r_0(ty_{0,i}))\), where only the jet of \(P\) below degree \(k\) enters (threshold-ideal lemma, part 1). It reports the cumulative rank of these value vectors. The point \(y_0\) is the next three outputs of mt19937_64 with the given seed (seed 1 here), drawn after the cone point \((\tau,\sigma)\), reduced modulo \(q\). The kernel now prints it in this mode, without changing the random stream. If \(\rho\) solutions have value rank \(\rho\) at \(y_0\), a \(\rho\times\rho\) minor of their coordinate matrix is nonzero at \(y_0\), hence a nonzero polynomial, so they are independent over \(F(y)\).

Finite check (check:cube-value-rank-four-three, research/results/bmd-r80-four-three/). Over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\):

  • \((3,2)\), validation. The value ranks are 1, 2, 2 at excess 3, 4, 5, as the proved basis of excesses 3 and 4 requires.
  • \((4,3)\), \(m=18\). The dimensions are 1, 4, 10, 19 at excess 3 to 6, and the value ranks are 1, 2, 3, 3.
  • Exact dimensions over \(\mathbb Q\). bmd_cube_witness_rank_q gives 1, 4 and 10 at excess 3, 4 and 5, as over \(\mathbb F_q\).

The threshold at (4,3)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-four-three). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over fields of characteristic 1000003, the solution module at \((d,\rho)=(4,3)\), \(m=18\), is free on three solutions of excesses 3, 4, 5. Hence \(\ell_0(5,18)=B(4,3)=3\).

Proof. Let \(q=1000003\).

  • Over \(\mathbb F_q\). Since the value rank rises 1, 2, 3 at excess 3, 4, 5, there are solutions \(\bar u_3,\bar u_4,\bar u_5\) of these excesses whose values at \(y_0\) have rank 3. They are therefore independent over \(\mathbb F_q(y)\).
  • Over \(\mathbb Q\). For \(\ell=3,4,5\), the saturated integer lattices of the witness systems have rank equal to the dimension over \(\mathbb F_q\). So they reduce onto the kernels over \(\mathbb F_q\). The map from witness to solution is defined over \(\mathbb Z_{(q)}\) (\(r_0\) has integer coefficients, and \(L'(0)=-1\)). So there are rational solutions \(u_3,u_4,u_5\) reducing to \(\bar u_3,\bar u_4,\bar u_5\). Suppose \(\sum c_iu_i=0\) over \(\mathbb Q(y)\). Clearing denominators and contents gives polynomials \(c_i\in\mathbb Z[y]\) with no common prime factor in their coefficients. Their reduction is a nontrivial relation \(\sum\bar c_i\bar u_i=0\) over \(\mathbb F_q(y)\), which contradicts the previous step.
  • Basis. In both characteristics the excesses sum to \(3+4+5=12=4^2-1-\binom32=N(4,3)\). By the basis criterion, \(u_3,u_4,u_5\) are a basis globally and locally, and \(\ell_0\ge3\). The product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B(4,3)=3\), with partition \((2)\). \(\square\)

This is the first case of open statement 1 with \(\rho\ge3\). In degree terms, along \(m=18\) the savings are at least 5 exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge3\). The order-zero theorem gave only \(\ell\ge2\). No splitting datum and no order half are used.

The near-diagonal family

Along \(\rho=d-1\) the target is always \(B=3\) (\(j=1\), partition \((2)\)). Consecutive excesses \(3,4,\ldots,d+1\) sum to \(3(d-1)+\binom{d-1}2=\tfrac{(d-1)(d+4)}2\). This equals \(N(d,d-1)=d^2-1-\binom{d-1}2\) for every \(d\).

Conjecture (conj:cube-near-diagonal-generators). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), for every \(d\ge3\), the solution module at \((d,d-1)\), \(m=5d-2\), is free on generators of excesses \(3,4,\ldots,d+1\). Hence \(\ell_0(d+1,5d-2)=3\).

It holds for \(d=3\) (\((3,2)\)) and \(d=4\), both in characteristic 0 and 1000003. By the basis criterion it reduces to exhibiting \(d-1\) independent solutions of these excesses. One of them is the product \(P_2P_1^{d-2}\), whose excess is 3: the origin order of a product is the sum of the \(p^2-1\) over its parts, as in the vertex-line entry. It would settle the diagonal next to the proved case \(\rho=d\).

General statement. conj:cube-near-diagonal-generators, for every \(d\ge3\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the basis criterion, part 1 of the threshold-ideal lemma (only the jet enters the solution), the product bound, and the lifting argument of the \((5,2)\) theorem, applied here to all three excesses. Claim searches (value rank, independence at a point, near-diagonal, \(\rho=d-1\)) found no earlier version. Checks: the value mode reproduces the \((3,2)\) basis, and the exact rational dimensions match the modular ones. A fresh-context referee checked the value computation (the series \(r_0\), the denominator, the index \(\ell+m-c\), the truncations), the independence certificate, the lifting through the three lattices, and the near-diagonal arithmetic. It found no gap. Its corrections are made: the characteristics of the proved near-diagonal cases, the evaluation point recorded, the characteristic-0 requirements in the assessment, the source for all even \(d\), and the product's excess cited.

Assessment. Evaluation at a random point certifies independence where cones cannot. So the basis method needs, per case, the dimensions and one evaluation over \(\mathbb F_q\), and for characteristic 0 also the exact ranks over \(\mathbb Q\) and the lattice lift. Open statement 1 is proved at \(\rho=2\) for all even \(d\) in every characteristic \(\ne2\) (theorem), and at \((3,2)\), \((5,2)\) and \((4,3)\) in characteristic 0 and 1000003. The generators beyond products are still found only by computation. The near-diagonal conjecture and the odd invariant generator are the two families where a construction would settle infinitely many cases.

26 September 2026 — The near-diagonal conjecture at d = 5: ℓ₀(6,23) = 3, and a diagonal conjecture on excesses 0, 2, …, d, checked at d = 2, 3

Working proof that ℓ₀(6,23) = B(5,4) = 3 in characteristic 0 and all but finitely many p, by a certified basis; a diagonal conjecture. Cycle bmd-r81. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The near-diagonal conjecture predicts that at \((d,d-1)\) the solution module is free on generators of excesses \(3,4,\ldots,d+1\). At \(d=5\), \(m=23\), that means value ranks 1, 2, 3, 4 at excess 3 to 6. A failure would be a rank below 4 at excess 6. The same method also asks what the generators on the diagonal \(\rho=d\) are. Products of lower generators could only produce the new near-diagonal generators if those are known.

Computations

Finite check (check:cube-value-rank-five-four, research/results/bmd-r81-five-four/). All runs use the val mode of bmd_cube_solution_cones over \(\mathbb F_{1000003}\), with seed 1 and the value point \(y_0=(10327,382842,84856)\) of the (4,3) entry. The "j=2" in the outputs is the kernel's jet-order parameter, not \(j=d-\rho\).

  • \((5,4)\), \(m=23\). The dimensions are 1, 4, 10, 20 at excess 3 to 6. As a consistency check only, this is the Hilbert function of \(\mathcal O(-3)\oplus\mathcal O(-4)\oplus\mathcal O(-5)\oplus\mathcal O(-6)\). The value ranks are 1, 2, 3, 4.
  • Exact dimensions over \(\mathbb Q\). bmd_cube_witness_rank_q gives 1, 4, 10, 20 at excess 3, 4, 5, 6, as over \(\mathbb F_q\).
  • The diagonal \((2,2)\), \(m=9\). The dimensions are 1, 3, 7, 13, 21, 31 at excess 0 to 5, and the value ranks are 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2.
  • The diagonal \((3,3)\), \(m=14\). The dimensions are 1, 3, 7, 14, 24, 37, 53 at excess 0 to 6, and the value ranks are 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3.

The threshold at (5,4)

Theorem (thm:cube-threshold-five-four). Over every field of characteristic 0, and over every field of characteristic \(p\) for all but finitely many primes \(p\), the solution module at \((d,\rho)=(5,4)\), \(m=23\), is free on four solutions of excesses 3, 4, 5, 6. Hence \(\ell_0(6,23)=B(5,4)=3\).

Proof. This is the proof of the (4,3) theorem with four excesses.

  • Over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(q=1000003\). The value rank rises 1, 2, 3, 4 at excess 3, 4, 5, 6. So there are solutions \(\bar u_3,\ldots,\bar u_6\) of these excesses whose values at \(y_0\) have rank 4. A \(4\times4\) minor of their coordinate matrix is nonzero at \(y_0\), so it is a nonzero polynomial, and they are independent over \(\mathbb F_q(y)\).
  • Over \(\mathbb Q\). At each excess 3 to 6 the dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) equals that over \(\mathbb F_q\). So the saturated integer lattice of each witness system reduces onto the kernel over \(\mathbb F_q\). The map from witness to solution is defined over \(\mathbb Z_{(q)}\). So rational solutions \(u_3,\ldots,u_6\) reduce to \(\bar u_3,\ldots,\bar u_6\). A relation over \(\mathbb Q(y)\) with coprime integral polynomial coefficients would reduce to a nontrivial relation over \(\mathbb F_q(y)\).
  • Other characteristics. Scale \(u_3,\ldots,u_6\) to integral vectors. A \(4\times4\) minor of their coordinate matrix is a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients. Let \(p\ne2\) be a prime not dividing its content. The entries of \(A_m\) lie in \(\mathbb Z[y]\), since \(r_0=L^{-1}\) has integer (Catalan) coefficients and \(L'(0)=-1\). So the reductions mod \(p\) are solutions over \(\mathbb F_p\). Each coordinate of degree \(a+m-c\) reduces to a form of that degree or to 0, so the excesses are kept. The minor commutes with reduction, so the reductions are independent over \(\mathbb F_p(y)\), and in particular nonzero. A nonzero polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\) stays nonzero over every field of characteristic \(p\).
  • Basis. In each of these characteristics the excesses sum to \(3+4+5+6=18=5^2-1-\binom42=N(5,4)\). By the basis criterion, \(u_3,\ldots,u_6\) are a basis globally and locally, and \(\ell_0\ge3\). The product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B(5,4)=3\). \(\square\)

Scope of the certified theorems. The prime 1000003 is only the modulus the kernels compute in. The computation there certifies independence over \(\mathbb Q\), but it does not limit the scope. The argument of the "other characteristics" bullet applies unchanged to the certified theorems at \((3,2)\), \((5,2)\) and \((4,3)\). Each of them proves rational solutions independent over \(\mathbb Q(y)\): at \((3,2)\) by the saturated lattices at excess 3, 4 and their degree-2 cones over \(\mathbb Q\), at \((5,2)\) by the lattice of the trivial part at excess 12, and at \((4,3)\) by the lattices at excess 3, 4, 5, so each threshold, with the freeness of its module, holds in characteristic 0 and in all but finitely many characteristics. At \((3,2)\) this covers the threshold and the basis of excesses 3, 4 (basis criterion entry), not the order half. The exceptional primes are 2 and those dividing the content of a chosen nonzero minor of the rational basis. They are not computed, so no particular small characteristic, such as 3, 5 or 7, is covered by these four theorems. Their recorded scope "characteristic 0 and 1000003" is correct but understates what the proofs give. So the near-diagonal conjecture holds for \(d=3,4,5\) in characteristic 0 and all but finitely many \(p\). In degree terms, along \(m=23\) the savings are at least 6 exactly for origin order \(\ell\ge3\).

The diagonal

On the diagonal \(\rho=d\) the threshold is \(B(d,d)=0\), which the record already proves. But the module structure is new. The excesses \(0,2,3,\ldots,d\) sum to \(\binom{d+1}2-1=\tfrac{(d+2)(d-1)}2\). This equals \(N(d,d)=d^2-1-\binom d2\) for every \(d\ge2\).

Observation. Modulo the computing prime 1000003, the solution module is free on generators of excesses 0, 2 at \((2,2)\) and 0, 2, 3 at \((3,3)\). No rational dimensions were computed here, so this is a finite check, not yet a statement in characteristic 0 or almost every \(p\). The lift of the theorem above would give both.

Proof. The value ranks give independent solutions of these excesses, as in the theorem above. Their excess sums are \(2=N(2,2)\) and \(5=N(3,3)\), so the basis criterion applies. \(\square\)

Conjecture (conj:cube-diagonal-generators). On \(\{0,1\}^3\) in characteristic \(\ne2\), for every \(d\ge2\), the solution module at \((d,d)\), \(m=5d-1\), is free on generators of excesses \(0,2,3,\ldots,d\).

Why the diagonal matters for the near-diagonal family. Here \(P_1\) is the boundary generator at \((1,1)\), of excess 0, and \(P_2\) the one at \((2,1)\), of excess 3. Products of witnesses are witnesses. Excesses add, and so do \(d\) and \(\rho\) (since \(m+1\) adds). The generator lists fit a product pattern:

  • At \((d,d-1)\) with \(d\ge4\), the excess lists are consistent with the near-diagonal generators as \(P_1\) times those of \((d-1,d-2)\), of excesses \(3,\ldots,d\), plus \(P_2\) times the diagonal generator of excess \(d-2\) at \((d-2,d-2)\), of excess \(d+1\). From \(d=6\) on, that factor is itself conjectural (the diagonal conjecture at \(d-2\ge4\)).
  • On the diagonal, for \(d\ge4\), the excess lists are consistent with \(P_1\) times the generators at \((d-1,d-1)\), plus the excess-2 generator at \((2,2)\) times the excess-\((d-2)\) generator at \((d-2,d-2)\). At \(d=4\) that is the square of the excess-2 generator at \((2,2)\).

This counts excesses only. Whether these products are independent is the open step. A product of witnesses is not yet a product of solutions, because the solution of a witness is only a window of its series. So it is not recorded as a reduction. At \(d=3\) the pattern does not apply: \((3,2)\) has a generator of excess 4 that is not a product, as the (3,2) entry found.

General statement. conj:cube-near-diagonal-generators and conj:cube-diagonal-generators, for every \(d\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the basis criterion, the proof of the (4,3) theorem (value certificate and lattice lift), and the product bound. Claim searches (diagonal generators, \(\rho=d\), freeness) found only the freeness conjecture, which names no excesses. A fresh-context referee checked every quoted number against the outputs, the values of \(N\) and \(B\), the certificate and the lift, and the excess and \((d,\rho)\) counts of the product pattern. It found no error. Its corrections are made: the title and the assessment limited to what is proved, the characteristic-0 part tied to equal rational dimensions, the factors of the product pattern named and its conjectural inputs marked, the Hilbert-function remark labelled a consistency check, and the kernel's parameter \(j\) explained. A second referee checked the extension to almost every \(p\): reduction of the equations, excesses and minor, and the passage to every field of characteristic \(p\). Its corrections are made: \(p\ne2\) explicit, the integrality of \(A_m\) sourced, the excess preservation stated, the lift step of each earlier theorem named, and the role of 1000003 stated precisely.

Assessment. The near-diagonal conjecture passed its first test beyond the cases that suggested it. It predicted exact value ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, and a rank of 3 at excess 6 would have refuted it. The diagonal is free on excesses 0, 2, …, d at \(d=2,3\) modulo the computing prime, and the counts suggest an induction through products. That needs a product on solution modules, and the independence of the products. Each further case of this family by computation adds only a finite check. The next step is a product construction that proves the family.

26 September 2026 — Small characteristics: a zero witness space transfers to characteristic 0, and the thresholds at (3,2), (4,3), (5,4) hold for p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13

Working proof of a transfer lemma; exact thresholds in characteristics 3 to 13; a conjecture that witness dimensions do not depend on the characteristic. Cycle bmd-r82. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The (5,4) entry extended the certified thresholds to all but finitely many characteristics, with the exceptions not computed. Which characteristics are exceptional? Small primes, and primes dividing \(d\), are where a genuine exception would appear, since the proofs pass through the \(d\)-division points of an elliptic curve. The test is an exact computation of \(\ell_0\) modulo each small prime. It ends with a value different from \(B\), or with agreement and a statement explaining it.

What "all but finitely many" gives

For one fixed \((d,\rho)\), agreement with characteristic 0 for all but finitely many \(p\) is automatic. \(\ell_0\) is decided by the ranks of finitely many matrices with integer entries, and each rank modulo \(p\) equals the rational rank except at the primes dividing some nonzero minor. So the extension in the (5,4) entry says nothing about any named prime. Its content there is the freeness of the module, not the threshold. The question is which primes are exceptional.

The transfer lemma

Write \(V_\ell(F)\) for the witness space at \((d,\rho)\) and excess \(\ell\) over a field \(F\): the polynomials of degree \(\le2k-d\), \(k=\ell+m+1\), with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices and origin order \(\ge\ell\).

Lemma (lem:cube-zero-space-transfer). On \(\{0,1\}^3\), let \(1\le\rho\le d\), \(m=4d+\rho-1\) and \(\ell\ge0\).

  1. \(\dim V_\ell(F)\) depends only on the characteristic of \(F\). It is at least its value in characteristic 0, with equality for all but finitely many \(p\).
  2. If \(V_\ell(F)=0\) for one field \(F\) of positive characteristic \(p\), then \(V_\ell=0\) in characteristic 0 and in all but finitely many characteristics. In each of these characteristics other than 2, \(\ell_0(d+1,m)>\ell\).

Proof. Part 1. The conditions are the vanishing of the Hasse derivatives \(\sum_b c_b\prod_i\binom{b_i}{\alpha_i}v_i^{b_i-\alpha_i}\) at the vertices \(v\), with \(|\alpha|<k\), and of the coefficients \(c_b\) with \(|b|<\ell\). So \(V_\ell(F)\) is the kernel of one matrix \(M\) with integer entries, reduced to \(F\). Its rank over \(F\) is its rank over the prime field, which is at most the rational rank. The two are equal unless \(p\) divides every \(r\times r\) minor, where \(r\) is the rational rank, that is, their gcd, which happens for finitely many \(p\).

Part 2. \(V_\ell(F)=0\) means that \(M\) has full column rank modulo \(p\). Then a maximal minor is nonzero modulo \(p\), hence nonzero over \(\mathbb Q\). So \(M\) has full column rank over \(\mathbb Q\) and modulo every prime not dividing that minor. By the threshold-ideal lemma, \((I^{(d+1)}_m)_{\ell'}\ne0\) exactly when some element of \(V_{\ell'}\) has origin order exactly \(\ell'\), that is, a nonzero degree-\(\ell'\) part (savings \(\ge d+1\) at \(k=\ell'+m+1\) means a witness of degree \(\le2k-d\)). Since \(I^{(d+1)}_m\) is a homogeneous ideal, a nonzero element in a degree \(\ell'\le\ell\) gives one in degree \(\ell\) after multiplication by a form of degree \(\ell-\ell'\). So \(V_\ell=0\) forces \((I^{(d+1)}_m)_{\ell'}=0\) for all \(\ell'\le\ell\), that is \(\ell_0(d+1,m)>\ell\). \(\square\)

So one computation modulo any single prime, showing that \(V_{B-1}=0\), proves \(\ell_0\ge B\) in characteristic 0. With the product bound this gives \(\ell_0=B\) there, without the lattice lift. The lift remains necessary for the freeness of the solution module. The lemma needs the whole space to vanish. A zero space of degree-\(\ell\) parts alone does not transfer, because a rational witness can have a degree-\(\ell\) part divisible by \(p\).

Exact computation in small characteristics

Kernel. research/tools/bmd_cube_solution_cones.cpp gains a mode series. For each prime of a list and each case \(d{:}\rho{:}\ell_{\min}{:}\ell_{\max}\), it computes \(\dim V_\ell(\mathbb F_p)\) after face division, which holds over every field. It also computes the dimension of the space of degree-\(\ell\) parts, which is positive exactly when \((I^{(d+1)}_m)_\ell\ne0\). Both are exact: no random point enters.

Result (research/results/bmd-r82-small-characteristics/). For \(p=3,5,7,11,13\) and \(1000003\), in each of the six cases below, \(V_{B-1}(\mathbb F_p)=0\), and \(V_B(\mathbb F_p)\) and its space of degree-\(B\) parts both have dimension 1. The dimensions do not depend on \(p\).

  • Controls, proved in every characteristic \(\ne2\): \((2,1)\) and \((3,1)\), where \(B=d^2-1=3,8\) (boundary theorem), and \((4,2)\), where \(B=6\) (theorem).
  • Certified cases: \((3,2)\), \((4,3)\), \((5,4)\), where \(B=3\). This includes \(p=3\) at \(d=3\) and \(p=5\) at \(d=5\), where \(p\) divides \(d\).

So over every field of characteristic 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13, \(\ell_0(4,13)=\ell_0(5,18)=\ell_0(6,23)=3\). Both bounds are the exact computation: \(V_2=0\) gives \(\ell_0\ge3\), and a nonzero degree-3 part gives \((I^{(d+1)}_m)_3\ne0\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), hence over every field of characteristic \(p\). By part 2 of the lemma, each of these computations also proves \(\ell_0\ge3\) in characteristic 0 on its own. This is registered as evidence for the conjecture below, not as a separate finite check, because the finisher caps new finite checks on this route.

Characteristic independence

Conjecture (conj:cube-characteristic-independence). On \(\{0,1\}^3\), for every \(1\le\rho\le d\) and \(\ell\ge0\), \(\dim V_\ell\) at \((d,\rho)\) is the same over every field of characteristic \(\ne2\). In particular \(\ell_0(d+1,4d+\rho-1)\) does not depend on the characteristic, and no characteristic other than 2 is exceptional for open statement 1.

Evidence: the 72 witness-space dimensions above (6 cases, 6 primes, \(\ell=B-1,B\)), which agree across six primes, and the rational dimensions at \((4,3)\) and \((5,4)\), which agree with those modulo 1000003. It is consistent with the dimension-three law, which gives the stable orders in every odd characteristic for \(n=3\). In dimension \(n\ge4\) the stable orders are proved only for \(p>2^{n-1}d\), and open statement 2 conjectures the same values at the small primes. The conjecture here is the analogue for the pre-stable thresholds of the cube.

General statement. lem:cube-zero-space-transfer, for every \((d,\rho,\ell)\), and conj:cube-characteristic-independence.

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the threshold-ideal lemma (the equivalence of savings with a nonzero element of \(I\), and its ideal property), face divisibility over every field, and the boundary and \((2e,2)\) theorems for the controls. Claim searches (characteristic independence, small primes, witness dimension) found no earlier version. A fresh-context referee checked the integrality of the system, the Hasse derivatives modulo \(p\), the origin order after face division, the series path of the kernel, every quoted number and the lemma's logic. It found no error. Its corrections are made: the space of degree-\(\ell\) parts claimed only to detect \((I)_\ell\ne0\), the upper bound in characteristics 3 to 13 taken from the computation, the unused hypothesis \(p\ne2\) dropped from part 2, the minor condition of part 1 stated exactly, the count of dimensions made precise, and the assessment narrowed to the cases computed.

Assessment. No prime from 3 to 13 is exceptional for these six cases at \(\ell=B-1\) and \(\ell=B\), including the primes dividing \(d\). Other \(\ell\) and other \((d,\rho)\) may still have small exceptional primes. The transfer lemma turns any single modular computation with \(V_{B-1}=0\) into a proof in characteristic 0. That makes the recorded computations of \(\ell_0\) cheaper to certify, but it proves nothing uniform in \(p\). A proof for every characteristic still needs a structural argument, as at \((2e,2)\). The record's computation of \(\alpha(Z)=B\) through \(d=7\) used a scheme system, not the witness spaces, so the lemma does not apply to it as it stands.

26 September 2026 — Witness products are products of functions on the curve: peeling by P₁ proves the diagonal and near-diagonal conjectures, and reduces each line d − ρ = j ≤ ρ to its start

Working proofs: a peeling lemma; ℓ₀ = 3 on ρ = d−1 and ℓ₀ = 6 on ρ = d−2 for every d, in characteristic 0 and all but finitely many p. Cycle bmd-r83. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, default reasoning).

Question. The near-diagonal and diagonal conjectures fit a product pattern in their excesses. The (5,4) entry left it unproved, because a product of witnesses was not known to be a product of solutions. Is there a product on solutions, and does it prove the pattern? The test ends with a proof for every \(d\), or with the step where the products fail.

Witnesses are functions on the curve

Setting. \(F\) is algebraically closed of characteristic \(\ne2\), and \(y\in F^3\) has distinct nonzero entries. \(C=C_a\), \(a=4y\), is the curve \(w_i^2=1+a_iT\) of the dimension-three law, of genus 1, with \(p_0=(1,1,1,0)\) and the four points \(H_\infty\) over \(T=\infty\). Put \(z_i=(1-w_i)/2\). Then \(L(z_i)=z_i^2-z_i=y_iT\), and near \(p_0\), \(z_i=r_0(y_iT)\) is the root curve, with \(L'(z_i)=-w_i\). For \((d,\rho)\) with \(1\le\rho\le d\) put \(m=4d+\rho-1\) and \(D_{d,\rho}=(m+1)p_0-dH_\infty\). A witness of excess \(\ell\) at \((d,\rho)\) is a polynomial \(P\in F[z_1,z_2,z_3]\), with coefficients independent of \(y\), of degree \(\le2k-d\), \(k=\ell+m+1\), with multiplicity \(\ge k\) at the seven nonzero vertices and origin order \(\ge\ell\). This is the definition of \(\delta_F\) in the goal with savings \(h=d+1\), since \(3+2k-2-h=2k-d\); the witness kernels of the (4,3) entry compute these spaces. Its solution is \(W^P_c=[T^{\ell+m-c}]\,P(z)/\prod_iL'(z_i)\), expanded at \(p_0\) (threshold-ideal lemma, part 1).

Lemma (lem:cube-witness-differential). Let \(\omega_0=dT/\prod_iL'(z_i)\).

  1. \(\omega_0\) is a regular differential on \(C\) without zeros.
  2. For a witness \(P\) of excess \(\ell\) at \((d,\rho)\), the function \(\varphi_P=T^{-k}P|_C\) lies in \(L(D_{d,\rho})\), and \(W^P_c=\operatorname{Res}_{p_0}(T^c\varphi_P\omega_0)\). So \(\varphi_P\) is the element that residue duality attaches to \(W^P(y)\).
  3. If \(P\) and \(Q\) are witnesses of excesses \(\ell_1,\ell_2\) at \((d_1,\rho_1)\) and \((d_2,\rho_2)\), then \(PQ\) is a witness of excess \(\ell_1+\ell_2\) at \((d_1+d_2,\rho_1+\rho_2)\), and \(\varphi_{PQ}=\varphi_P\varphi_Q\).

Proof. Part 1. \(T\) has degree 8. Over \(T=\infty\) and over each \(T=-1/a_i\) it has four points of ramification index 2, and elsewhere it is unramified. At a point over \(-1/a_i\), \(w_i\) is a local parameter, \(dT=2w_i\,dw_i/a_i\) has a simple zero, and \(w_i\) has a simple zero. At a point of \(H_\infty\), \(T\) has a pole of order 2, so \(dT\) has a pole of order 3, and each \(w_i\) has a simple pole, so \(\prod w_i\) has a pole of order 3. Elsewhere \(dT\) and \(\prod w_i\) have neither zeros nor poles. So \(\omega_0=-dT/\prod w_i\) has no zeros or poles.

Part 2. \(T\) vanishes exactly at the eight points over \(T=0\), where \(w\in\{\pm1\}^3\), that is, \(z\in\{0,1\}^3\). It is unramified there, so it is a local parameter at each of them. At a nonzero vertex, \(P\) has multiplicity \(\ge k\), so \(P|_C\) vanishes to order \(\ge k\), and \(\varphi_P\) is regular. At \(p_0\) (\(z=0\)), \(P|_C\) vanishes to order \(\ge\ell\), so \(\varphi_P\) has a pole of order \(\le k-\ell=m+1\). At a point of \(H_\infty\), each \(z_i\) has a simple pole, so \(P|_C\) has a pole of order \(\le2k-d\), and \(T^{-k}\) vanishes to order \(2k\), so \(\varphi_P\) vanishes to order \(\ge d\). \(\varphi_P\) is regular elsewhere. So \(\varphi_P\in L(D_{d,\rho})\). Finally \(\operatorname{Res}_{p_0}(T^cT^{-k}P\,dT/\prod L'(z_i))\) is the coefficient of \(T^{k-c-1}=T^{\ell+m-c}\) in \(P/\prod L'(z_i)\), which is \(W^P_c\). Residue duality is injective, so \(\varphi_P\) is its element.

Part 3. Degrees, vertex multiplicities and origin orders add, and \(2k_1-d_1+2k_2-d_2=2k-d\) with \(k=k_1+k_2\), \(d=d_1+d_2\). Since \(m+1=k-\ell\), the values of \(m+1\) add, so \(m=m_1+m_2+1=4d+(\rho_1+\rho_2)-1\). And \(\varphi_{PQ}=T^{-k_1-k_2}PQ=\varphi_P\varphi_Q\). \(\square\)

Since \(L(z_i)=y_iT\) on \(C\), and \(L(z_i)\) vanishes at every vertex, has origin order 1 and degree 2, the product \(L(z_i)P\) is a witness of excess \(\ell+1\) at \((d,\rho)\) with \(\varphi_{L(z_i)P}=y_i\varphi_P\). So \(y_iW^P=W^{L(z_i)P}\), and \(S\)-multiples of witness solutions are witness solutions.

So witness products are products in the function field of \(C\). They are well defined on solutions, since \(\varphi_P\) depends only on \(W^P(y)\), and they carry polynomial solutions to polynomial solutions.

The peeling lemma

Let \(P_1\) be the witness of the boundary generator at \((1,1)\), of excess 0. Its function \(\varphi_1\) spans \(L(5p_0-H_\infty)\), a divisor class of degree 1, so \(\operatorname{div}\varphi_1=H_\infty+q_1-5p_0\) for one point \(q_1=q_1(y)\). Call a solution a witness solution if it is \(W^P\) for a witness \(P\).

Lemma (lem:cube-peeling). Over a field of characteristic \(\ne2\), let \(2\le\rho\le d\).

  1. Suppose the solution module at \((d-1,\rho-1)\) is free on witness solutions \(u_1,\ldots,u_{\rho-1}\) of excesses \(a_i\). Let \(h\) be a witness solution at \((d,\rho)\) of excess \(2d-\rho\), not in the \(F(y)\)-span of the \(P_1u_i\). Then the solution module at \((d,\rho)\) is free on \(P_1u_1,\ldots,P_1u_{\rho-1},h\), and \(\ell_0(d+1,m)\ge\min(a_1,\ldots,a_{\rho-1},2d-\rho)\).
  2. For \(y\) in a dense open set, \(q_1(y)\notin H_\infty\cup\{p_0\}\). There, in the setting of part 1, a witness solution \(h\) at \((d,\rho)\) lies in the \(F(y)\)-span of the \(P_1u_i\) if and only if \(\varphi_h(q_1(y))=0\) for all \(y\) in a dense set.

Proof. Independence over \(F(y)\) and membership in an \(F(y)\)-span do not change when \(F\) is replaced by its algebraic closure, so assume \(F\) algebraically closed, as residue duality and the points \(q_1(y)\) require.

Part 1. By the forward direction of the basis criterion (the recorded degree identity), \(\sum a_i=N(d-1,\rho-1)\). Also \(N(d,\rho)-N(d-1,\rho-1)=2d-1-(\rho-1)=2d-\rho\). By part 3 of the witness-differential lemma the \(P_1u_i\) are witness solutions at \((d,\rho)\) of excesses \(a_i\), since \(P_1\) has excess 0. So the \(\rho\) solutions have excess sum \(N(d,\rho)\). They are independent over \(F(y)\): at a point \(y\) where the \(u_i(y)\) are independent (a dense open set), the \(\varphi_{u_i}\) are independent, and so are the \(\varphi_1\varphi_{u_i}\), since \(\varphi_1\ne0\) in the function field. With \(h\) outside their span, the basis criterion gives a basis, and its part 3 gives \(\ell_0\ge\min\).

Part 2. \(q_1\ne p_0\): otherwise \(H_\infty\sim4p_0\), that is, \(c=[H_\infty-4p_0]=0\). The coprimality lemma shows that \(c(y)=0\) forces the top coordinate \(F_1\) of the boundary solution at \(d=1\) to vanish, where that solution is nonzero, and \(F_1\) is a nonzero constant. Next, \(P_1\) has degree exactly 9 \(=2k-d\): otherwise \(\varphi_1\) would vanish to order \(\ge2\) at all four points of \(H_\infty\), and \(\operatorname{div}\varphi_1\ge2H_\infty-5p_0\), of degree 3, is impossible. Let \(\tau\ne0\) be its top-degree form. At the point of \(H_\infty\) with \(w_i\sim\varepsilon_i\sqrt{a_iT}\), the direction of \(z\) is \((\varepsilon_i\sqrt{a_i})\), and \(\varphi_1\) vanishes there to order exactly 1 when \(\tau(\varepsilon_1\sqrt{a_1},\varepsilon_2\sqrt{a_2},\varepsilon_3\sqrt{a_3})\ne0\). The product of these eight values is a polynomial in \(a\). It is not identically zero, since at \(a_i=t_i^2\) it is \(\prod_\varepsilon\tau(\varepsilon t)\) and \(\tau\ne0\). So for \(y\) in a dense open set, \(\varphi_1\) has simple zeros on \(H_\infty\) and \(q_1\notin H_\infty\).

At such \(y\), where also the \(u_i(y)\) are independent and hence a basis of the solutions at \((d-1,\rho-1)\) by dimension, residue duality and part 2 of the witness-differential lemma give \(\operatorname{span}\{P_1u_i(y)\}\leftrightarrow\varphi_1L(D_{d-1,\rho-1})\). Here \(D_{d,\rho}-D_{d-1,\rho-1}=5p_0-H_\infty\). So \(\chi\in L(D_{d-1,\rho-1})\) exactly when \(\operatorname{div}(\varphi_1\chi)\ge-D_{d,\rho}+q_1\). Since \(q_1\notin\operatorname{supp}D_{d,\rho}\), this says that \(\varphi_1\chi\in L(D_{d,\rho})\) vanishes at \(q_1\). So \(h(y)\) is in the span exactly when \(\varphi_h(q_1)=0\). If \(h\) is in the \(F(y)\)-span, this holds on a dense open set. Conversely, if it holds on a dense set, the \(\rho\) solutions are dependent at every point of that set, so a \(\rho\times\rho\) minor vanishes there, hence identically. On the good open set, the locus \(\varphi_h(q_1(y))=0\) is the common zero set of the \(\rho\times\rho\) minors of \((P_1u_1,\ldots,P_1u_{\rho-1},h)\), so it is closed there. Hence if \(h\) is outside the span, \(\varphi_h(q_1(y))\ne0\) on a dense open set, since \(y\)-space is irreducible. \(\square\)

The diagonal and the near-diagonal family

Theorem (thm:cube-diagonal-near-diagonal). Let \(F\) have characteristic \(\ne2\). Suppose that in \(F\):

  • (i) there is a witness solution \(g_2\) of excess 2 at \((2,2)\), not in \(F(y)P_1^2\);
  • (ii) there is a witness solution \(g_3\) of excess 3 at \((3,3)\), not in the \(F(y)\)-span of \(P_1^3\) and \(P_1g_2\).

Then for every \(e\ge2\) the solution module at \((e,e)\) is free on witness solutions of excesses \(0,2,3,\ldots,e\). If moreover (iii) the solution module at \((3,2)\) is free on witness solutions of excesses 3 and 4, then for every \(d\ge3\) the solution module at \((d,d-1)\) is free on witness solutions of excesses \(3,4,\ldots,d+1\), and \(\ell_0(d+1,5d-2)=3\).

Proof. Diagonal. At \((1,1)\) the module is free on the solution of \(P_1\) (boundary theorem, \(\rho=1\)). Apply the peeling lemma with \(\rho=d=e\), where \(2e-\rho=e\):

  • \(e=2\): \(h=g_2\), outside \(F(y)P_1\cdot P_1\) by (i).
  • \(e=3\): \(h=g_3\). The basis at \((2,2)\) is \(P_1^2,g_2\), so the \(P_1\)-images are \(P_1^3,P_1g_2\), and (ii) applies.
  • \(e\ge4\): \(h=g_e:=g_2g_{e-2}\), a witness solution of excess \(e\) at \((e,e)\) by part 3 of the witness-differential lemma. By part 2 of the peeling lemma, the previous steps give \(\varphi_{g_2}(q_1)\ne0\) and \(\varphi_{g_{e-2}}(q_1)\ne0\) on dense open sets. So \(\varphi_{g_e}(q_1)=\varphi_{g_2}(q_1)\varphi_{g_{e-2}}(q_1)\ne0\) on their intersection, and \(g_e\) is outside the span.

By induction the excesses are those at \((e-1,e-1)\) together with \(e\), that is, \(0,2,\ldots,e\).

Near-diagonal. The case \(d=3\) is (iii). For \(d\ge4\) take \(h=P_2\,g_{d-2}\), where \(P_2\) is the boundary witness at \((2,1)\), of excess 3. It is a witness solution at \((d,d-1)\) of excess \(d+1=2d-\rho\). Its function is \(\varphi_{P_2}\varphi_{g_{d-2}}\). \(\varphi_{P_2}\) spans \(L(9p_0-2H_\infty)\), so \(\operatorname{div}\varphi_{P_2}=2H_\infty+q_2-9p_0\). Where \(q_1\notin H_\infty\cup\{p_0\}\), \(\varphi_{P_2}(q_1)=0\) would force \(q_1=q_2\). Then \(5p_0-H_\infty\sim9p_0-2H_\infty\), that is, \(c=0\), which is excluded. And \(\varphi_{g_{d-2}}(q_1)\ne0\) generically by the diagonal part, since \(d-2\ge2\). So \(h\) is outside the span, and the peeling lemma adds excess \(d+1\) to the excesses \(3,\ldots,d\) at \((d-1,d-2)\). So \(\ell_0\ge3\), and the product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B(d,d-1)=3\). \(\square\)

Corollary. Over every field of characteristic 0, and of characteristic \(p\) for all \(p\) outside one finite set that does not depend on \(d\), the diagonal conjecture holds for every \(e\ge2\) and the near-diagonal conjecture for every \(d\ge3\). In particular \(\ell_0(d+1,5d-2)=B(d,d-1)=3\) for every \(d\ge3\).

Proof. The hypotheses (i), (ii), (iii) are statements about finitely many solutions.

  • (iii). The (3,2) theorem and the basis criterion entry give rational witness solutions of excesses 3 and 4, independent over \(\mathbb Q(y)\), with excess sum \(7=N(3,2)\).
  • (i), (ii). Modulo \(q=1000003\), the value ranks at the point \(y_0\) of the (5,4) entry are 1, 1, 2 at excess 0 to 2 at \((2,2)\), and 1, 1, 2, 3 at excess 0 to 3 at \((3,3)\). The witness spaces have dimensions 1, 3, 7 and 1, 3, 7, 14 over \(\mathbb F_q\), and the exact rational dimensions (bmd_cube_witness_rank_q, research/results/bmd-r83-peeling/) are the same. At \((2,2)\) excess 2, the dimension \(7=6+1\) is \(S_2P_1^2\) plus one more solution \(\bar g_2\), whose value at \(y_0\) is independent of \(P_1^2(y_0)\), by the rank 2. At \((3,3)\) excess 2, \(7=6+1\) is \(S_2P_1^3\) plus \(P_1\bar g_2\). The latter is not in the former, since \(\varphi_1\varphi_{\bar g_2}\) and \(\varphi_1^3\) are independent. So the value span of excess \(\le2\) at \(y_0\) is that of \(P_1^3(y_0)\) and \(P_1\bar g_2(y_0)\). The rank 3 at excess 3 gives \(\bar g_3\) with a nonzero \(3\times3\) value minor against them. As in the (4,3) theorem, the saturated witness lattices reduce onto the modular spaces, so \(\bar g_2,\bar g_3\) lift to integral witnesses \(g_2,g_3\). The \(2\times2\) minor of \((P_1^2,g_2)\) and the \(3\times3\) minor of \((P_1^3,P_1g_2,g_3)\) are integral polynomials, nonzero modulo \(q\), hence nonzero over \(\mathbb Q\).

This gives characteristic 0. For characteristic \(p\), reduce the finitely many integral witnesses modulo \(p\), as in the (5,4) theorem. The needed independences are these two minors and one for \((3,2)\), with integer coefficients, and they survive outside the primes dividing their contents. Together with 2, these primes form the finite exceptional set. \(\square\)

The values match the recorded computations: at \((4,3)\) the generators are \(P_1\) times the \((3,2)\) basis (excesses 3, 4) and \(P_2g_2\) (excess 5), and at \((5,4)\) they are \(P_1\) times those and \(P_2g_3\) (excess 6).

Each line reduces to its start

For \(\rho\ge j=d-\rho\), open statement 1 has \(q=\min(\rho,j)=j\), and the balanced partition of \(j+q=2j\) into \(j\) parts is \((2,\ldots,2)\), so \(B(d,\rho)=3j\). In the product bound this is the product \(P_2^{\,j}P_1^{\,\rho-j}\), from the partition of \(d\) into \(\rho\) parts with \(j\) parts 2 and \(\rho-j\) parts 1, of excess \(3j+0\). Only this upper bound is used. Call \((2j,j)\) the start of the line \(d-\rho=j\).

Theorem (thm:cube-peeling-lines). Let \(F\) satisfy (i), (ii), (iii) of the theorem above, and let \(j\ge1\). Suppose the solution module at \((2j,j)\) is free on witness solutions whose least excess is \(3j\). Then for every \(\rho\ge j\) the module at \((j+\rho,\rho)\) is free on \(P_1^{\,\rho-j}\) times the generators at the start, the \(P_1\)-multiples of the earlier new generators, and new generators of excesses \(3j+1,\ldots,2j+\rho\), and \(\ell_0(j+\rho+1,\,4(j+\rho)+\rho-1)=3j=B\).

Proof. Let \(u_4\) be the generator of excess 4 at \((3,2)\). The excess-3 generator there is \(P_1P_2\), because the module at \((2,1)\) is free on the solution of \(P_2\) (boundary theorem). So \(u_4\) is outside \(F(y)P_1\cdot P_2\), and by part 2 of the peeling lemma \(\varphi_{u_4}(q_1)\ne0\) generically. Induct on \(s=\rho-j\), applying the peeling lemma at \((d,\rho)=(2j+s,j+s)\), where \(2d-\rho=3j+s\):

  • \(s=1\): \(h=P_2^{\,j-1}u_4\). It lies at \((2(j-1)+3,(j-1)+2)=(2j+1,j+1)\), with excess \(3(j-1)+4=3j+1\). For \(j=1\) it is \(u_4\) itself.
  • \(s\ge2\): \(h=P_2^{\,j}g_s\), with \(g_s\) the diagonal generator of excess \(s\) at \((s,s)\). It lies at \((2j+s,j+s)\), with excess \(3j+s\).

In both cases \(\varphi_h(q_1)\) is a product of \(\varphi_{P_2}(q_1)\ne0\), \(\varphi_{u_4}(q_1)\) and \(\varphi_{g_s}(q_1)\), each nonzero on a dense open set. So \(h\) is outside the \(P_1\)-span, and the module at \((2j+s,j+s)\) is free on the \(P_1\)-multiples of the previous generators and \(h\). All generators are witness solutions. Their least excess is \(\min(3j,3j+1)=3j\), so \(\ell_0\ge3j\), and the product bound gives \(\ell_0\le B=3j\). \(\square\)

Corollary. In characteristic 0 and all but finitely many \(p\) (the exceptional set of the corollary above), \(\ell_0(d+1,5d-3)=B(d,d-2)=6\) for every \(d\ge4\).

Proof. Take \(j=2\). At \((4,2)\) the module is free on the witness solutions of \(P_2^2\) and \(P_3P_1\), of excesses 6 and 8 (theorem, every characteristic \(\ne2\)). The least excess is \(6=3j\). \(\square\)

For \(j=1\) the theorem, started at the boundary case \((2,1)\), is the near-diagonal part above. The line \(j=2\) agrees with the recorded values 6 at \((5,3)\), \((6,4)\) and \((7,5)\). So in the region \(\rho\ge d-\rho\), open statement 1 reduces to the starts \((2j,j)\) with \(j\ge3\): freeness there with least excess \(3j\).

General statement. lem:cube-witness-differential, lem:cube-peeling, thm:cube-diagonal-near-diagonal and thm:cube-peeling-lines, for every \(d\) and \(j\).

Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: residue duality, the threshold-ideal lemma (the solution of a jet), the curve \(C_a\) of the dimension-three law, the basis criterion and its forward direction, the coprimality lemma (\(c\ne0\) where \(F_1\) is constant), the boundary theorem, the \((2e,2)\) theorem, the product bound, and the lifting argument of the \((4,3)\) and \((5,4)\) theorems. Claim searches (product of solutions, witness differential, peeling, multiplication, hyperplane) found only residue duality and the conjectures this entry proves. Checks: the rational dimensions at \((2,2)\) and \((3,3)\) equal the modular ones. A fresh-context referee checked the witness solution formula against the threshold-ideal lemma, the divisors of \(\omega_0\) and \(\varphi_P\), products, both parts of the peeling lemma, the induction and the lifts, and found that the record does not already imply the results. Its corrections are made: hypotheses (i), (ii) restated as the independences the proof uses, with a \(2\times2\) and a \(3\times3\) minor as certificate; the open-set direction of peeling part 2; the source of the witness definition, with \(y\)-independent coefficients and \(S\)-multiples; and the passage to the algebraic closure. A second pass on the line theorem checked its steps and the start \((4,2)\). Its corrections are made: the value \(B=3j\) derived from the record's definition and the product used, and the generators named as \(P_1\)-multiples.

Assessment. This is the first infinite family inside open statement 1 with \(\rho\ge3\). It turns the near-diagonal and diagonal conjectures into theorems in characteristic 0 and almost every characteristic. The key is that witnesses are functions on the curve \(C_a\), so their products are products of functions, and multiplication by \(P_1\) carves out the hyperplane of solutions vanishing at one point \(q_1\). The new generators on every line come from \(P_2\), \(u_4\) and the diagonal, so each line \(d-\rho=j\le\rho\) reduces to its start \((2j,j)\). The lines \(j=1,2\) are now complete outside a finite set of characteristics. The remaining cases of open statement 1 are the starts with \(j\ge3\), and the region \(\rho<j\), which peeling does not reach.
